item.title: The conscience files
item.dc:creator: Aeon Video
item.description:
The sorrows and redemptions of visitors who mailed their ‘souvenirs’ back to Arizona’s Petrified Forest National Park

- by Aeon Video

Watch on Aeon
item.content:encoded:
The Petrified Forest National Park in Arizona is so named for its unique and plentiful petrified wood, formed from conifer trees that lived there some 225 million years ago. As more than 500,000 people visit the park each year, inevitably, not all heed the US National Park Service’s guidance to ‘take only photographs, leave only footprints’. And, as the acclaimed short documentary The Conscience Files explores, a small but not insignificant number of visitors come to deeply regret their decision, taking it upon themselves to return the stolen rocks via mail, and provide a written explanation. Some even come to believe a long-circulating rumour about the park: those who steal rocks from the land are cursed.

For the film, the US director Brian Bolster was given access to the park’s archive of these letters, which blame the ‘curse’ for everything from the deaths of loved ones to the outbreak of a family stomach bug. Some are lighthearted and others are tragic. However, what most share is the need to unburden a guilty conscience and a desire to assign cause and meaning to the bad things that life seems to arbitrarily dole out. Pairing readings of these letters with scenic views of the park, what emerges is a rich, panoramic portrait of both the place and humanity itself.

item.title: In praise of zealotry
item.dc:creator: Geertje Bol
item.description:
Early feminists like Mary Astell and Catharine Macaulay refused their male peers’ advice to remain polite in debate. Why?

- by Geertje Bol

Read on Aeon
item.content:encoded:
Listen to this essay

25 minute listen

In 1706, an English woman visited her friend, Katherine. Katherine’s husband, Francis Atterbury, was a prominent politician and bishop. Upon hearing that Francis had just finished writing his sermon, Katherine’s friend asked if she could take it home to read it. Francis graciously agreed, no doubt expecting to receive some compliments from the lady. But his sermon was promptly returned to him by the woman with copious criticism and notes for its improvement. Francis was shocked: he complained to a friend that the lady lacked a ‘decent manner’ and that she was ‘offensive and shocking in her expressions’. He admitted: ‘I dread to engage her.’

This ‘indecent’ and ‘shocking’ woman was Mary Astell (1666-1731). Today, she is best known as England’s first feminist, whose paradoxical mix of conservative politics and pioneering feminism has long puzzled scholars. By 1706, Astell was no doubt used to being called offensive, irritating and impolite. She wrote most of her partisan pamphlets in the first decade of the 18th century, always studded with sharp attacks on men she disagreed with (often, but not exclusively, those on the side of the Whig liberals, the most famous of which was John Locke). One of the pamphleteers she attacked, James Owen, dismissed her as overly angry, zealous and ‘virulent’ – a dismissal that meant that he did not have to actually engage with her sharp and difficult arguments.

More than half a century later, another politically active woman received similar treatment. The historian and political theorist Catharine Macaulay (1731-91) had penned a sharp pamphlet attacking Edmund Burke, who remains widely received as the ‘father’ of modern conservatism and the first major proponent of organised political parties. Macaulay had taken issue with Burke’s now-famous defence of party, Thoughts on the Cause of the Present Discontents (1770). Instead of dealing with her critique head on, Burke wrote to his friend that ‘the Amazon is the greatest champion amongst them … no heroine in Billingsgate can go beyond the patriotick scolding of our republican Virago.’ Invoking the image of the fierce female warrior and of the loud, masculinised woman, he ridiculed Macaulay, but not without a sense of awe. Much like Atterbury, Burke admitted he was ‘afraid to answer her’.

But Burke’s dismissal of Macaulay was not just rudeness – it was entirely consistent with his broader vision of what partisanship should look like, and who should be allowed to practise it. In the very tract that sparked Macaulay’s attack, Burke argued that partisanship is best conceived of as a well-chosen, loyal friendship between polite, reasonable and like-minded men, who agreed with one another ‘at least nine times in ten’. Only in this way could partisanship exist ‘without violating concord’. By contrast, Macaulay’s pamphlet was impolite, fierce and zealous. In Burke’s eyes, then, Macaulay’s brand of partisanship certainly violated concord and harmony.

Burke was not the only 18th-century theorist to champion politeness, friendship, moderation and reasonableness. David Hume, too, stressed the importance of concord. A partisan shouldn’t be too principled; he should be able to ‘easily agree with his fellow-citizen’. Righteous partisans were ‘more zealous’ and ‘more furious and enraged’ than those who were reasonable and prone to compromise. Anthony Ashley-Cooper, the third Earl of Shaftesbury also thought it was crucial to safeguard concord. For this purpose, he recommended the cultivation of ‘serene, soft, and harmonious’ manners to combat angry, zealous political ‘warfare’. The message of these men was clear: partisans should be polite, reasonable, moderate and friendly. Only then could partisanship make politics better – that is, more harmonious. Only then could partisanship, as it were, be tamed. Impolite, zealous, angry, and righteous voices like those of Astell and Macaulay were threatening precisely because they disrupted concord.

What makes Astell and Macaulay’s shared experience all the more striking is that they came from opposite ends of the political spectrum. Where Astell was a Tory conservative defender of the Church of England, absolute monarchy and religious orthodoxy, Macaulay was a radical republican and Whig, championing popular sovereignty, religious toleration and revolution. But despite disagreeing on nearly everything, they arrived at remarkably similar views on how to do partisan politics. This suggests that their insight arose not from their partisan commitments but from their shared position on the margins. As women, neither could vote nor hold public office, and partisanship – writing pamphlets, joining political groups, intervening in public debates – was one of the few avenues of political participation available to them.

Their experience as women and partisans allowed them to see what the more fully politically included men around them couldn’t

We might expect Astell and Macaulay to have defended themselves against the likes of Atterbury, Owen and Burke by arguing that they were not in fact impolite or zealous or offensive. But, instead, they embraced these monikers. In her pamphlet Moderation Truly Stated (1704), Astell gladly admitted that she liberally ‘sprinkled’ her writing with ‘my inflaming Oratory, Satyr and Invective’. Unlike men such as Owen, Shaftesbury or Atterbury, she preferred the honest ‘Quintessence of Gall’ over the flattering, soothing ‘Extract of Honey’. Even if truths were hurtful or shocking, it was still preferable to dole them out rather than to hold back. ‘[I]f there appears any Bitterness in’ her own writings, Astell said, ‘it arises only from the Plainness and Force of Truth, which ill Men cannot bear.’ Macaulay similarly adopted an unapologetic attitude to men like Burke or Hume who found her shockingly honest and direct: the point of being a partisan was ‘to speak some bold offending truths’. Even if it caused one ‘to be very offensive’ and ‘obnoxious’, it was still preferable to dishonest politeness.

Why did Astell and Macaulay reject those ‘virtues’ that their male peers extolled? Their experience as women and partisans allowed them to see what the more fully politically included men around them couldn’t: that insisting that partisans be polite, moderate, reasonable and friendly would actually serve to exclude marginalised political voices. It could do so in two ways.

First, there was the problem of gatekeeping. As Astell put it: ‘Who shall be the Judge’ of what and who counted as (im)polite, (im)moderate, and (un)reasonable? It would be the powerful and fully politically included men like Shaftesbury who would be the judge. Paraphrasing Shaftesbury’s ‘Letter Concerning Enthusiasm’ (1708), Astell suggested he had argued that wit and ridicule were acceptable, provided ‘we treat it with Good Manners’. But while men like Shaftesbury might be able to dole out ridicule wherever they went and still be considered polite and well-mannered, women like Astell would, for the very same behaviour, be berated for their bad manners. In her last pamphlet, t (1709), Astell challenged Shaftesbury by asking whether women or servants would be allowed to ‘treat the Master of the Family in this Fashion?’ In other words, while powerful men would be allowed to behave however they liked and still be deemed well-mannered and reasonable, servants, women and other ‘Person[s] of No-Figure’ would not. In her book Mere Civility (2017), the political theorist Teresa Bejan shows that thick conceptions of early modern civility functioned in exactly this way – excluding dissenting voices by raising the threshold for civility so high that only insiders could meet it. But where Bejan proposes a thinner, more minimal form of civility, Astell and Macaulay went further.

Astell and Macaulay identified another problem: voices at the margins of politics had special cause to be righteous and zealous. On important issues – such as the equality of the sexes – it would not do to remain polite or seek a moderate compromise. Macaulay faced precisely this problem with Burke: he argued that only those involved in the daily practice of politics were qualified to make political judgments. By contrast, ‘speculative’ thinkers like Macaulay, who were not included in the thick of politics, were naive and unfit. They ‘soften[ed] into a credulity below the milkiness of infancy’. They could perhaps reason about the ‘ends of government’ but not with the practical means of it. Macaulay refused to accept this: she argued that her distance from power actually gave her superior insight vis-à-vis fully included partisans.

In her 1770 reply to Burke, Macaulay argued that ‘practical gentlemen’ like himself were too corrupted by self-interest and political power to make unbiased political judgments. But with some healthy distance, ‘speculative thinkers’ like Macaulay could think more clearly and were better equipped to spot the ‘sinister views’ of those in the thick of politics. A ‘moderate’ response to Burke would have been to concede that both sides have some important political insight – indeed, this was what he himself gestured at. But Macaulay refused to meet Burke on the middle ground, because the middle ground would still effectively silence her political voice. When it came to arguments about who was included and who excluded, it would not do to be polite, reasonable and moderate. For someone in Macaulay’s position, zeal and righteousness were not character flaws, but the only adequate response to a system that defined her out of legitimate political speech.

Astell agreed. Whereas, throughout the 18th century, people tended to define zeal as ‘excessive or immoderate enthusiasm’, she praised the ‘Zealot’, who was ‘warm and assiduous’ and ‘stiff and narrow-Spirited’. Astell’s subversive point was that inflexibility in one’s principles and beliefs was admirable – on important matters, from religion to women’s position in society, it was wrong to be quickly dissuaded, or to change one’s mind too readily: ‘an Honest Man’ had an ‘Inflexible Conscience’ and did not ‘Veer with the Times’. When it came to politics, it was important to take sides. And if the ‘Honest man’ thought the other side had a good point, then ‘he ought to go over to them.’ Macaulay, too, praised partisans with ‘inflexible attachment to the cause’, and who were ‘actuated by so warm and honest a zeal’. Righteous zeal meant taking a decided stance, not looking for middle ground, and zealously arguing one’s cause. It was directly opposed to the political virtues their male peers recommended.

Far from destroying political debate, righteous, zealous partisans in fact sustained it

To Astell and Macaulay, it was obvious that, in political debate, righteous zeal was preferable. First of all because partisans on the margins had most to lose from moderate, polite reasonableness. If they politely conceded that their opponents had a point, nothing ever changed. These virtues would only maintain the status quo, whereas Astell and Macaulay sought to challenge and change it. Astell wanted to combat the pernicious and ill-grounded ‘customs’ – a term that closely resembles our present-day idea of ‘social norms’ – that painted women as inferior creatures, incapable of political argument and devoid of intellect. ‘Custom, that merciless torrent that carries all before it’ needed to be checked. Macaulay likewise worried that ‘the generality of mankind are too fond of accustomed establishments’, and therefore ‘interested to reject every part of reformation’. Partisanship was a powerful means available to those on the margins – those who could never belong to Burke’s ‘practical gentlemen’ involved in daily politics – seeking to challenge the prejudices and norms that tried to keep them out. The philosopher Myisha Cherry makes a parallel argument in her book The Case for Rage (2021), writing that righteous anger was a driving force in the civil rights movement – a context where polite, moderate appeals for equality had long failed to produce change.

Accepting righteous zeal instead of polite, moderate reasonableness was more inclusive: it allowed for a greater number of people to make their voices heard and be taken seriously. But Astell and Macaulay also argued that, far from destroying political debate, righteous, zealous partisans in fact sustained it. After all, these ‘warm’ and ‘inflexible’ people kept arguing with their opponents even when it was unwelcome. As a righteous, zealous partisan herself, Astell envisioned meeting her ‘enemies in heaven hereafter’ where ‘they shall be sensible that their admission is in some measure owing to our own importunate intercessions for them’. In other words, it was only due to her constant arguments and persuasions that her opponents would improve themselves and their views. ‘This,’ she mused in her magnum opus The Christian Religion (1705), ‘will be no doubt a sweet revenge.’ Macaulay seems to have been a persistent political interlocutor too. An acquaintance of hers said that ‘though she plays at cards and talks of different subjects,’ she ‘always returns’ to politics, even at parties – ‘an odd character for a lady’.

Since righteous, zealous partisans favoured honesty over politeness, they were also happy to risk causing offence in pursuit of persuasion. Macaulay argued that, just as tyranny stood opposed to liberty, so zeal stood opposed to formality, or ‘outward appearance or semblance’ and ‘conformity to established rule’. For Macaulay, zeal thus implied a disregard of outward appearance or conformity. To be zealous often meant being bold, truthful, even impolite. As Astell put it, it involved ‘speaking truths which no man would say’, in other words, speaking ‘the Truth that wounds’.

At this point, the image of zealous, righteous partisans trying to persuade one another might conjure up worrying images of shouting without any genuine dialogue taking place. Even if such partisans would keep talking, would they really listen to one another? Astell and Macaulay’s writings show that they did in fact always take their opponents’ views seriously. Their most partisan and zealous works often targeted one or two men they disagreed with: they went through their arguments, one by one, including references to page numbers and quotations, and explained why they were wrong on all counts. In her pamphlet Moderation Truly Stated, Astell gave Owen this treatment – whereas Owen, the proponent of moderation and reasonableness, dismissed Astell’s entire work in one sentence. Macaulay’s two responses to Burke also engaged with his arguments in depth, whereas Burke ridiculed her but never deigned to respond to her arguments. This wasn’t a coincidence. A righteous, zealous partisan who wanted to persuade her opponents had to take their arguments seriously; whereas a polite, moderate partisan who valued concord over truth could afford to dismiss an uncomfortable, controversial voice and move on.

Today, righteous, zealous partisans seem as unreasonable as they are incapable of changing their minds. And what is the point of political debate if no one ever changes their mind? But to Astell and Macaulay, righteous zeal was compatible with a degree of open-mindedness and critical thinking. They certainly did not consider all standpoints as equally valid, but nonetheless took them seriously. Both Astell and Macaulay praised inflexibility and were wary of partisans whose views swayed with the wind. As the philosopher Lea Ypi points out, not being quick to change one’s mind can actually bolster political commitment and can ensure that partisan projects persist over time. In other words, it can ensure that partisans don’t give up too easily.

But even if partisans should be somewhat inflexible, would righteous zeal not foreclose the very possibility of open-mindedness? If we define it as taking every other standpoint as equally valid, then righteous, zealous partisans would indeed not be open-minded. But if we define it, as the philosopher Jeremy Fantl does in The Limitations of the Open Mind (2018), as the willingness ‘to pull back on your confidence if I offer an argument each step of which you find compelling and in which you cannot, by your own admission, find a flaw,’ then righteous zeal is certainly compatible with open-mindedness. Astell believed that, if a member of the Church of England did not think that dissenters were mistaken, ‘he ought to go over to them’. A partisan’s righteousness should never prevent them from looking critically at their own beliefs, nor preclude a change of mind: Astell advised her readers to ‘receive no man’s opinion on his bare word, nor to swallow his arguments without examining them.’

It is affective polarisation, not disagreement itself, that actually threatens political debate

What’s more, Astell and Macaulay’s rejection of partisanship as friendship actually protects against echo chambers. It is the moderate, friendship-based model that we find in Burke that risks groupthink, because loyalty to one’s friends and a desire to avoid offence prevents frank disagreement. Astell wrote that these friends ‘expect to be followed right or wrong in their principles, party, and passions’, and wished to ‘be flattered’. They would not ‘tell you of your Faults for fear of disobliging you’. By contrast, Astell and Macaulay were not only critical to partisans of opposing sides, but also criticised their co-partisans: Astell critiqued the Tory Charles Davenant in Moderation Truly Stated, and Macaulay had a disagreement with the fellow radical John Wilkes. Both women had a decided preference for open, honest enemies over ‘concealed enemies’ in the guise of friends. In other words, if you surround yourself with polite, loyal friends who flatter you and avoid offence, your views never get tested; if you engage honestly with your opponents who challenge you in turn, they do.

That this vindication of righteous zeal came from two women, not from the men who dominated partisan theory, is no accident. To forgo righteousness and zeal in the face of deep disagreement is a luxury not available to all – least of all to those positioned at the margins of politics. Likewise, to insist that partisans should dispense with righteousness and zeal in favour of reasonableness, politeness and moderation is itself a privilege. As Astell and Macaulay pointed out, it risks excluding or persecuting those who are most oppressed in politics, and who have most need of, and cause for, righteous zeal.

Astell and Macaulay’s diagnosis is especially urgent today, when we hear calls for more moderate, reasonable, polite debate from all sides of the political spectrum as the cure for polarisation. But the terms of what counts as reasonable political speech are still set by insiders, and voices expressing righteousness, zeal or anger are still viewed as threats to democratic life rather than as contributions to it. Just as in the 18th century, today this also works to silence partisan voices on the margins – those with most need of righteous zeal. It is certainly true that righteous zeal is unlikely to reduce ideological polarisation – where partisans move away from the centre. But the mere fact of such polarisation need not be detrimental to politics. Righteous zeal can combat a more worrying form of polarisation, affective polarisation – the refusal to engage with one’s opponents at all. And it is affective polarisation, not disagreement itself, that actually threatens political debate.

Perhaps in an ideal world, where everyone is equally included, and where everyone’s voices are heard, we wouldn’t need righteous, zealous partisans. But that is not the world we live in. Political life remains marked by deep inequalities of voice and standing. Insisting on politeness, moderation and reasonableness may make political debate more harmonious among those already fully included. Yet it simultaneously silences those on the margins – and bringing in a wider array of voices is precisely what is needed to improve political debate. Writing from the margins, Astell and Macaulay show us that righteous zeal is not a threat to politics, but rather a condition of genuine political inclusion and frank political debate.

item.title: The World Famous Gopher Hole Museum
item.dc:creator: Aeon Video
item.description:
In this bittersweet portrait of a farm town in Canada, taxidermied gophers preserve a place that no longer exists

- by Aeon Video

Watch on Aeon
item.content:encoded: This short documentary is an oddly endearing portrait of Torrington, a hamlet in Alberta, Canada, and the institution at its heart: the World Famous Gopher Hole Museum. Opened in 1996, the tourist attraction features taxidermied Richardson’s ground squirrels assembled into hand-crafted dioramas that recreate scenes from the town’s past – including its many shops and gathering places. The film’s guide is Dianne Kurta, the museum’s long-time curator, who at the time of filming was stepping back due to health issues. As she showcases dioramas depicting a Torrington that no longer exists, the film shifts from a quirky small-town portrait into a bittersweet meditation on the struggle to remember and be remembered, and the inevitability of change.

item.title: Worm munch matters
item.dc:creator: Ella Browning
item.description:
The lives that slither and scurry beneath the soil’s surface are vital for ecological health: now we can listen in to them

- by Ella Browning

Read on Aeon
item.content:encoded:
Listen to this essay

22 minute listen

Earthworms do not have a discernible mouth, a means to make sound, or ears, and most spend their lives burrowing below ground, eating soil and decaying organic matter. However, their behaviours produce sounds, which can reveal a surprising amount about the subterranean world in which they live. I’ve recently found myself leaning over a box of soil in the basement of my university department, headphones clutched to my ears, revelling in the soft, Velcro-like scrapes of earthworms eating. It sounds like this:

I have always loved earthworms. As a child on my parents’ allotment, I delighted in finding them in the soil as potatoes were dug in, fascinated by their soft, alien form wiggling in my hand. Now, I amuse my friends by ducking down in crowds at music festivals to rescue distressed earthworms from being squashed by the mob of muddy boots.

Until recently, my scientific research focused on the rapid patter and chop of bat echolocation calls, monitoring how their populations were responding to largely human-driven environmental change. I didn’t consider that the same ecoacoustic approaches could be applied below ground, to understand how earthworms are affected by us surface-dwellers. Fortunately, others had. I finally had a way to connect my scientific research speciality with my ardour for earthworms in the soil.

Worm munch might seem like a curiosity, but it represents a much bigger change in how we understand nature. More than just the behaviour of single creatures, such sounds can also reveal the health of whole ecosystems – and the underground is emerging as a new acoustic frontier.

Sound itself is a wave, a travelling vibration. Vibrancy is a word often used to describe colour and life. A vibrant ecosystem, therefore, is one that hums with the sounds of life.

While reading this essay, you can listen to a 15-minute recording of various sounds of the underground, collected in Oxfordshire in 2024:

Monitoring nature’s sounds has a long history. The ancient Greeks wrote poems and plays about birdsong and, in medieval England, the sounds of local birds gave many places their names. Today, an expert ornithologist will stand in a forest and conduct a bird survey using nothing but their eyes and ears.

However, when bioacoustics researchers in the 20th century began to place microphones or hydrophones and recorders in the field for days, weeks or months – known as ‘passive acoustic monitoring’ – they discovered whole new natural soundscapes. This technique has been especially powerful in realms where humans cannot stay for long, or for species that emit infrasonic or ultrasonic sounds beyond human hearing range (20-20,000 Hz).

Underwater habitats, for example, are difficult for people to be immersed in for extended periods without specialist equipment and training (for obvious reasons). Thus, collecting data on animals like whales and dolphins, which can traverse vast oceanic distances, was historically done with sightings from land or boats. That changed with passive acoustic sensors.

Bats use the returning echoes of their ultrasonic calls to build a sonic map of their surroundings

In the 1950s during the Cold War, the US Navy developed its Sound Surveillance System (SOSUS), an underwater network of hydrophones with the purpose of tracking Soviet submarines in the Atlantic and Pacific oceans, originally code-named ‘Project Jezebel’. Arrays of hydrophones were deployed on the seafloor, connected via cables to the shore where the acoustic data could be monitored. While an original premise of this system was upheld – that enemy submarines would be easily tracked by their low-frequency sound signatures – the assumption that there would be little other noise in the ocean was not true. Sailors operating the SOSUS detected many other unknown sounds, including one they attributed to the ‘Jezebel Monster’. It took some years and the detective work of marine bioacousticians for this to be identified as the 20 Hz call of fin whales. Many other mysterious sounds began to be discovered, including the ‘boing sound’ and the ‘lightsabre sound’, both of which were also eventually attributed to minke whales. Since many cetaceans use sound for day-to-day activities – ranging from the low-frequency songs of blue whales to the whistles and high-frequency echolocation clicks of bottlenose dolphins – hydrophone technology has enabled these animals to be more fully understood as they move through the ocean.

Passive acoustic technology was similarly illuminating in demystifying bats and revealing one of their incredibly sophisticated evolutionary adaptations. Nearly all bats are nocturnal, relatively small, fly fast, and vocalise at frequencies mainly outside of human hearing, all of which makes them effectively invisible to people, or has caused them to be associated with evil and hence feared. Unless you’re looking for bats, you’re unlikely to notice them (although admittedly this is not true of larger fruit bats, which are hard to miss in parts of the world where they can congregate in cities in large numbers).

In the 1930s, the American physicist George W Pierce developed a method for detecting ultrasound using piezoelectric crystals and a sonic amplifier to study the ultrasonic sounds of birds and crickets. When the Harvard undergraduate Donald Griffin – who was convinced that bats were using sound for navigation – brought a cage of bats to Pierce’s lab, they discovered a cacophony of ultrasonic sound. Further research by Griffin and others revealed the full complexity of bats’ use of ultrasound, showing they used the returning echoes of their ultrasonic calls to build a sonic map of their surroundings, orienting themselves during rapid flight. Griffin termed this ‘echolocation’ – and ever since then it has allowed us to better understand the sonic world of the bat, which before was hidden in plain sight.

Although bioacoustic sounds have now been studied for decades, it’s only relatively recently that scientists have begun to use soundscapes to gauge ecosystem health, with the establishment of the field of ‘ecoacoustics’ in 2014. Ecoacoustics incorporates parts of bioacoustics, but also draws on the ideas of ‘soundscape ecology’, which traces back to the 1960s. As well as ‘biophony’ (animal sounds), ecoacoustics also incorporates geophony (sounds made by wind, rain, waves) and anthropophony (sounds made by humans or human activities).

A core principle of ecoacoustics is that complexly noisy natural places are healthier natural places. This means that it’s not just the volume of noise, but the diversity of sound that indicates habitat health. The dawn chorus in an intact Bornean tropical forest is magical in its complexity, especially if you’re lucky to experience it mixed in with the whoops of a troop of gibbons swinging through overhead, as I was during a visit in 2019.

In contrast, cities are generally not ecologically healthy and, while they are incredibly noisy places, they are filled with the harsh, more monotonous sounds of car engines and other machines, and often little biotic sound. Soundscapes dominated by anthropogenic sounds have been linked to poor mental health in people, whereas the opposite has been found for natural sounds like birdsong or forest soundscapes.

Carson demonstrated that the lack of spring’s dawn chorus in the US was due to the accumulation of DDT

A biotically silent landscape is a sign of nature collapse, as exemplified in Rachel Carson’s Silent Spring (1962):

Over increasingly large areas of the United States, spring now comes unheralded by the return of the birds, and the early mornings are strangely silent where once they were filled with the beauty of bird song.

Collating scientific research, Carson demonstrated that the lack of spring’s dawn chorus in the US was due to the accumulation of DDT, a synthetic pesticide. DDT caused the thinning of bird eggshells and thus reproductive failure. Without Carson publicising the alarm of a silent landscape, resulting in the eventual ban of DDT in the US, many bird species may have been lost.

While the ecoacoustics of forests or cities are relatively straightforward to monitor, the underground world is more difficult to access. Monitoring earthworms and other soil-based creatures presents a similar challenge to listening to whales in the deep ocean or bats in the dark sky: there’s only so much an ear to the ground can hear. Yet by inserting acoustic probes or burying hydrophones into the soil, it’s possible to hear the rustling cacophony of an ant’s nest, the clicks of beetle larvae communication, and the scrapes of earthworm engineering.

Before I began listening in earnest to the underground, I almost solely used passive acoustic sensors to record bat echolocation and social calls, gleaning information on which species were where, how they were using different habitats, and how human actions were impacting their populations. I grew comfortable in this ultrasonic world and could pick out bat calls almost instantly when listening to recordings (slowed down to bring them into our hearing range), looking at a spectrogram. Transferring these skills to the low, soft sounds in the soil has been somewhat of a sonic culture shock.

The first time I listened to a soil soundscape, it felt like taking my first steps into an alien world. I’d spent so many years focusing on identifying sounds above ground, and now I had a portal into this earthy realm and a whole new acoustic space. Much of our recordings contain periods of little noise or near silence, punctuated by the unpredictable shuffles of something moving or something eating. I began to feel like Jodie Foster’s character Dr Ellie Arroway in the film Contact (1997), spending hours listening, searching for signals to decode and link to a biotic source or anthropogenic activity. Instead of ticking off in my head what the sources of the sounds might be, I’m often perplexed, imagining what the faunal, or otherwise, origins of the scratches, sifts, drums and buzzes could be.

We found post-midnight peaks in acoustic activity when earthworms are most active in the soil, and higher diversity under rewilded grassland

Here are two examples, one of which sounds like a laser, and the other like something buzzing:

Soil is the foundation of many ecosystems above ground: the medium from which plants grow, and the basis of most food chains. However, it also comprises complex ecosystems itself, filled with a high diversity of fauna, from microscopic bacteria to carnivorous mammals, which impact soil structure, function and chemical composition. And we’re finding that a healthy soil is often a noisier one.

Early results from studies using passive acoustics to assess soil health in garden, forest and farmland ecosystems have proved promising. Researchers have found associations between forest recovery and ecoacoustic measurements of soil soundscapes, suggesting healthy soils do sound significantly different. In my own research, we are testing the use of passive acoustic monitoring for assessing soil health and the effectiveness of nature recovery approaches in UK grassland landscapes. Unlike previous soil ecoacoustic projects, we have collected continuous 24-hour recordings across our sites, which has revealed dynamic patterns in the soundscapes from day to night. We found post-midnight peaks in acoustic activity when earthworms are most active in the soil, and higher diversity under rewilded grassland, compared with intensively grazed cattle pasture. Concurrent to the ecoacoustic data, we conducted traditional soil biodiversity sampling, scooping up large and tiny soil-dwelling animals, such as earthworms, ants, woodlice, millipedes, beetles and insect larvae. Earthworms made up most of the soil invertebrates, and we believe their movements are contributing significantly to the soil soundscape.

Why? Earthworms are soil ecosystem engineers. Their burrows change the soil structure, and different types of earthworms have different burrowing behaviours – vertical or horizontal, deep or shallow – which allow air and water to flow. Earthworms also break down dead plant and animal matter into smaller pieces, which are fed on by bacteria and fungi, releasing nutrients that would otherwise be trapped. That’s why counting earthworms is a common method for assessing soil health in agricultural settings.

To meet internationally agreed goals for biodiversity restoration, we need systematic and standardised ways to monitor soil health. Traditional techniques require costly manual effort, followed by laboratory analysis for chemical indicators, such as pH and nutrient availability, or physical indicators, such as water-holding capacity, texture and compactness, or biological indicators, such as soil enzymes, microbial biomass and diversity, and soil carbon. The effort means such tests can be conducted only at relatively small scale, sampling only snapshots of the soil.

Passive acoustic sensors, by contrast, can be buried in the soil and left to collect data over multiple days, with multiple sensors buried simultaneously in different locations. A healthy soil where natural biological processes are intact will sound different to a depleted or chemically scarred soil due to the differences in diversity and abundance of animals living in it, the physical properties, and resulting structure. At least that’s the ecoacoustic theory.

Since underground ecoacoustics is a young field, we’re still ironing out details, discovering unknowns, and encountering challenges. Firstly, some ecoacoustic methods for analysing environmental soundscapes are based on the premise that audible biotic sounds are made between 2,000-15,000 Hz and anthropogenic sounds between 1,000-2,000 Hz. This was defined on the frequency range of bird calls, but it already causes headaches for researchers in areas with a lot of anthropogenic sounds, such as cities, where machines emit sounds across the frequency spectrum. The problem may be particularly acute in soil ecoacoustics, because much of the sounds we’re recording are between 1,000-3,000 Hz, spanning both the ecoacoustically defined biotic and anthropogenic categories.

A second thing we’re learning is that only a small fraction of soil organisms are acoustically detectable. Unlike bats or crickets or frogs or whales, earthworms and other soil organisms do not shout to find their way around, nor trill and whoop to attract mates. In fact, earthworms don’t make any deliberate sounds at all. Movement sounds alone are incredibly difficult to assign to specific species as they don’t have a function, like bat echolocation. However, if we can link some of these soil sounds to broad functional groups, this will give us better insight into soil health and above-ground habitat, enabling us to unpick what is driving differences between sites.

We are on the cusp of unearthing and understanding a subterranean soundscape never heard before

A third major challenge is the lack of available libraries on soil faunal sounds with which to verify signals in our recordings. However, we are starting to build these. While others are focusing on beetle sounds, such as those made by dung beetles under cow pats, we have started with the earthworms. By listening to earthworms in a bespoke soundproof worm habitat (a 0.5 m3 wooden box covered in soundproof foam and filled with soil), with no other fauna present, we can confirm we’re hearing the same worms in the field.

1 of 4

We also still need to unpick confounding factors that affect the soil soundscape. For instance, the impact of soil type and moisture on sound transmission is not well known, yet it will impact the sounds recorded. The dispersion of sound in the soil is complicated. Fortunately, there is a significant body of research outside ecoacoustics, focusing on detecting cracks in oil pipes and similar important, buried infrastructure, that has tackled this problem. So work is underway to translate this to our field.

Finally, there are the physical challenges. Soil type and moisture also affect the ability to actually get the acoustic sensors into the soil. In July 2025, a couple of students and I were conducting a small-scale soil ecoacoustic survey on a Cotswolds-based regenerative farm; temperatures were above 30°C and it hadn’t rained for weeks. The ground was rock solid, making digging the roughly 10 cm-deep holes for the hydrophones incredibly difficult. It took us bouncing on top of spades like pogo sticks to make any headway. We ran into a further extreme weather-related challenge with the effect of high heat on the recorder’s portable battery, which drained power quicker than anticipated.

However, all of this is part of the learning process with new field techniques. And the bigger picture? We are on the cusp of unearthing and understanding a subterranean soundscape never heard before.

Sound is a tangible way of connecting to aspects of nature that are hidden from humans. The deep ocean, the dark night, and now the dense earth beneath our feet. Listening to realms that may seem devoid of life invokes new understanding and can highlight the vibrancy of life, thriving in overlooked places.

What other uncanny sounds will we encounter in the subterranean realm, and what might they tell us about nature recovery? Like the oceanic hydrophone network, eventually we could have a Soil Sound Surveillance System (a SOSOSUS, if you will) buried in fields, woodlands, savannahs and moorlands, monitoring the hidden world beneath our feet. Maybe we’ll discover an underground ‘Jezebel Monster’.

‘What is it like to be a bat?’ was the question posed by the philosopher Thomas Nagel, in his essay about understanding the experiences of others and differences in perception. Bioacoustics opened up the world of bat echolocation and sonic sensory experience. Perhaps, through understanding sonic vibrations in the soil, we can unlock an experience even more alien than a bat’s, prompting the question: What is it like to be an earthworm?

item.title: The neverending house
item.dc:creator: Consuelo Araos
item.description:
The self-built homes of Santiago are precarious and ever changing. They are, always and at once, being and becoming

- by Consuelo Araos

Read on Aeon
item.content:encoded:
Listen to this essay

24 minute listen

Few problems feel more pressing today than housing. Across the world, access to affordable, stable, dignified housing has become one of the defining challenges of our time, in wealthy capitals and struggling peripheries alike. According to UN-Habitat, more than 2.8 billion people – roughly 35 per cent of the global population – lack access to adequate housing. Rents rise faster than wages; ownership recedes as an aspiration for younger generations; entire neighbourhoods are reshaped by speculation and displacement. The question of who gets to live where, and on what terms, sits at the heart of contemporary urban life.

This is not a new problem. In The Housing Question (1872), Friedrich Engels identified it as a structural consequence of industrial capitalism: as workers flooded into cities, the market and the state proved incapable of providing, or unwilling to provide, shelter for all. From that moment, housing became a political question. Over the following century, governments across the developed world came to assume that the solution lay in their hands: through public construction, regulation, subsidy, and the organised machinery of mortgage markets and mass homeownership. Housing was a problem to be solved – technically, bureaucratically and financially. Today, that problem has only deepened: a global crisis of affordability and tenure grips cities across the world, and housing is drawn ever further into the circuits of finance and speculation.

Yet across much of the 20th century, in the rapidly urbanising cities of Latin America, Africa and Asia, the state-led housing paradigm never fully took hold. Cities grew faster than any state or real-estate market could manage. Millions gained access to housing – and to the city itself – not through the formal mechanisms of policy and planning, but by occupying land, building by hand and gradually, generation by generation, turning bare earth into home, in ways that the state variously resisted, tolerated, regularised or actively supported. In countless such cities, self-built houses and neighbourhoods were not an exception to the urban order; they were intrinsic to how the city was made.

The precariousness, informality and lack of top-down planning that characterise access to shelter in the cities of the Global South may well justify seeing them as a failure – a sign of governments’ and societies’ inability to adequately resolve the housing question. And yet, somewhat paradoxically, it is precisely among self-built environments that housing can be seen from an angle rarely present in mainstream debate, and nonetheless fundamental: that any serious attempt to understand how societies provide a place to live must first ask what it means to live somewhere at all, and what role the house itself plays in that. In simple words, that behind every housing problem lies a dwelling problem. Behind the pervasive technical illusion of the house as object, commodity and asset, the building-dwelling bond tends to disappear. By contrast, in self-building, that relationship remains exposed and alive, woven into the life that the house makes possible, and that makes the house possible in return. Two decades of fieldwork in the urban margins of Chile’s capital Santiago have led me to see, in this little-by-little, intergenerational, unfinished way of making one’s own house, an experience of building that has something to teach us about the art of dwelling.

I came to the question of the house long before I had any concepts for it. Victoria worked in my family’s home when I was a child and, for as long as I can remember, I knew her through the story of her own house – a story I first overheard in her conversations with my mother, and which years later, when I began my first fieldwork on domestic life in Santiago, became the first I set out to study, and the one I have returned to ever since. Her house was Victoria’s favourite subject of conversation. Whenever we talked, it would intrude everywhere: in anecdotes, in complaints, in memories, even in the most ordinary exchanges about almost anything.

Victoria was already an older woman when I first interviewed her in 2007, early in what would become ongoing fieldwork on domestic life in Santiago. She had retired some years earlier, after a lifetime as a domestic worker, due to advanced diabetes. Born in a very poor village of seaweed gatherers, Victoria ran away as a child from the foster family her birth mother had placed her with. She barely attended school, and while still an adolescent she joined her life to the man who would become her husband. With him she had six children – the first before she turned 15; the youngest, disabled, already in his 40s – and she became a great-grandmother before 50.

Four generations had lived under Victoria’s roof – by rearranging rooms or by adding new ones in the backyard and on top of the house

If many of the topics we discussed were, for her, a source of complaint – particularly those concerning her health and the everyday tensions among her relatives – Victoria seemed to take a particular, almost contagious pleasure in describing the smallest details of how the house had been built from the moment they arrived, when the plot was ‘nothing but bare earth’, as well as its successive transformations and its ongoing plans, improvements and repairs.

I was struck by her meticulous attention to materiality and to specific quantities – a sack of cement, two sheets of corrugated zinc, 10 metal bars for the gate – the exact inputs she and her husband were constantly using. Certain words began to acquire a new meaning for me in this context. They were ‘closing’ (cerrando) the plot – building the wall that separates the house from the street. They needed to ‘line’ (forrar) the interior wooden walls – adding a second layer of boards to insulate them better. She spoke of needing to ‘raise’ (levantar) the kitchen floor, of building a terrace; at one point she had had to ‘raise the radier’ – to cover the concrete slab with an additional layer of cement. She dreamed of ‘finishing’ (terminar) the bathroom, which she had never managed to build entirely in material – by which she meant cement and brick, as opposed to wood, which was not considered a proper material because it was not as solid and durable. These were often long-term and discontinuous processes, unfolding in stages and marked by pauses and resumptions.

The neverending story of the making of Victoria’s house was intimately intertwined with another story that unfolded in our conversations: the gradual and constantly reconfigured settlement of her children’s families. Over time, as many as four generations lived under Victoria’s roof – whether by rearranging existing rooms or by adding new ones in the backyard and on top of the house. Such intertwining of materiality and relatedness becomes especially clear in a conversation with one of her daughters. A few years earlier, after three decades in her mother’s home, she had moved to a small, rented house behind another property nearby, in order to make space for her own grandchildren. ‘If you have problems,’ she said to me, ‘the only place to go is your mother’s. If my husband tells me to leave, I come back here. You know that your parents will always open the door to you. My parents have never closed their doors to their children – never.’

And yet the same house that never closes its door can also close in. Victoria, who took such pleasure in recounting how it was built, spoke of those years in another register too: ‘crowded together’ (todos amontonados), ‘you cannot fight for your life, fight for yourself’. She still dreamed of the terrace, the small garden, the raised kitchen floor she never had room to finish. Here one glimpses the enduring strength of the moral expectation to welcome one’s children, and the extent to which home-leaving is understood as reversible. The house appears as something pliable – and that pliability cuts both ways. It can crowd and exhaust as readily as it can shelter; but because it is never finished, it holds the conflict open, as something that might yet be eased by a room added at the back, a wall moved, a life rearranged. A ‘definitive house’ forecloses that wager. The self-built one keeps it alive – for better and for worse.

Victoria’s story is part of a broader reality among poor urban populations across Latin America, where roughly a quarter to a third of urban residents have lived in informal housing conditions as cities expanded through the late 20th and early 21st century. In Santiago, much of what is now the pericentral belt took shape between the 1960s and ’80s through a precarious process of informal occupation of marginal land and later state-regularised poblaciones that shaped the city’s growth. These are neighbourhoods slowly and collectively assembled by hand over multiple generations – their houses, streets and public spaces still bearing the marks of that history, as do the family configurations and forms of local sociability, as well as civic and political participation, that took shape within them.

Although it may be technically correct to consider the self-built house as merely one particular residential typology among others, I have come to think otherwise. I arrived with the vocabulary of deficit – informality, overcrowding, the housing unit to be counted and completed – and the field slowly took it apart. In all their precariousness – and perhaps partly because of it – self-built houses reveal some conditions without which a place cannot truly be lived as a house. These are conditions just as present, though far harder to see, in the finished and affluent houses I have also studied across Santiago. This is why I see the self-built dwelling not as a type but as an archetype of housing – not because it is exemplary, but because it is revealing: in it, what every house already is becomes visible.

I found a philosophical grounding for this intuition in Martin Heidegger’s essay ‘Building Dwelling Thinking’ (1951), in which he reflects on the deeper relation between dwelling and building in order to illuminate what he calls the plight of dwelling in our time. The text was first delivered as a lecture at the Darmstadt Colloquium, a gathering of architects, philosophers and intellectuals convened in the context of the postwar reconstruction of a defeated and devastated Germany. The colloquium took place at a moment of intense pressure to industrialise construction and address a massive housing shortage. The question at stake was whether reconstruction should be guided primarily by technical efficiency and standardisation, or whether the problem ran deeper – touching on the very meaning of dwelling in the modern age. What Heidegger diagnosed in relation to industrialised building has since been intensified by the financialisation of housing.

These houses remain open and adaptable. They are built slowly alongside the making of kinship and personhood

Heidegger’s argument begins by acknowledging the widespread – and understandable – urgency to build large numbers of houses. Construction becomes the object of diagnoses, planning schemes, industrial coordination and commercial enterprise, all directed toward the efficient production of dwelling units. In this framework, building appears as a technical and economic task, and houses as functional objects designed to provide shelter. Against this backdrop, Heidegger shifts the question. However acute the housing shortage, he writes, the ‘real plight of dwelling’ does not lie simply in the lack of houses, but in the fact that we have yet to learn how to dwell. Building efficiently doesn’t guarantee that what is built can be truly lived in.

Within the technical paradigm, dwelling and building appear as sequential: we build in order to dwell. Heidegger reverses the assumption. We build because we dwell. This is not simply a reversal of cause and effect. It is a more radical claim: dwelling has ontological priority. It names the fundamental way in which mortals are upon the earth. He grounds this claim in language itself: the modern German bauen (‘to build’) derives from the Old High German buan, which originally meant to remain in a place – to dwell – and is related to bin, ‘I am’. At its root, building already belongs to dwelling. The priority of dwelling is therefore ontological: it names the fundamental way in which mortals are upon the earth.

In much of the contemporary world, houses are delivered as finished products – ready to be inhabited, financed and exchanged. Within this technical paradigm, the house exists as a completed object, externally related to those who later occupy it. Life enters a structure already defined.

By contrast, in contexts of self-construction, a house’s becoming is interwoven with the events that shape its inhabitants’ lives – expected or unforeseen, welcome or distressing. These houses remain open and adaptable. They are built slowly alongside the making of kinship and personhood. Floors are raised when money allows; walls are lined later; rooms are added as children grow, couples separate, grandchildren arrive. Small piles of cement, timber or corrugated sheets often sit in the corners of a plot – materials acquired when possible, signs of a future still under construction. Through an irregular rhythm of gifts, loans and shared labour, houses and persons become durably linked. Because the house remains unfinished, it becomes the horizon within which aspirations and frustrations, projects and setbacks take shape.

The contrast with Chile’s social housing regime since the 1980s is striking. In official jargon, the dwelling delivered by the state is a vivienda definitiva – a ‘definitive house’. Designed as complete units with limited scope for expansion, these houses are granted once in a lifetime, regardless of a family’s position in the life cycle. Residential trajectories are anchored to a single institutional event. Those who have already received a subsidy are even described as ‘marked’.

A second dimension becomes visible in the way houses and persons are bound together through kinship and co-residence. In the technical paradigm, the house exists first; inhabitants enter later. In self-construction, this separation collapses. The history of a house’s construction is inseparable from the relationships that made it possible. Materials circulate among relatives; labour is lent and returned; rooms are added not only to accommodate bodies but to sustain bonds. But the same circulation can be refused, and to refuse it is to refuse the bond. When Victoria began to ‘close’ her plot – to build the wall onto the street – she asked her son-in-law for a sack of cement, or two. He sent word back that he could put nothing on a plot that was not his. ‘That was a hard blow,’ she said. To withhold the cement was to withhold the relationship.

In Victoria’s case, children and grandchildren moved in and out as circumstances required. What might appear as overcrowding from the outside was locally understood as obligation and continuity. Building does not merely provide a setting for kinship; it gives it material form. To add a room ‘at the back’ or ‘above’ is not only a spatial act but a relational one. Distance and proximity, autonomy and dependence, conflict and reconciliation are built into the arrangement of rooms, thresholds and passages. Over time, several dwellings may differentiate within what was once a single house – small ‘independent’ units drawn from the original structure. The plot becomes a constellation of related domestic spaces, linked by shared histories of construction and inhabitation. The house is not simply where relatedness unfolds; it is one of the means through which it is realised.

A third dimension concerns the relation between house and land. In many of Santiago’s peripheries, the house begins not with construction but with occupation. Before there was a wall or roof, there was a plot described as ‘nothing but bare earth’. The foundational gesture was taking and holding a piece of land.

Rosa’s story makes this visible in another way. Her wooden house stood on stilts embedded in the slopes of the Chicauma hill. Years earlier, someone had offered her the plot precisely because no one else wanted it: settling there meant ‘ganársela al cerro’ – winning the ground from the hill. ‘Every day I would come up here,’ she told me, ‘and clear a little ground; then, when my husband got back from work, he would come and do a little more.’ This is how houses are made here: de a poquito, little by little. A neighbour gave her a small shack, three metres by three, to set down and ‘secure the plot’. Each winter, heavy rains could undo what had been built. The domestication of the hill was never definitive.

To level the ground, mark boundaries and raise a first shelter is not merely preparatory to building; it is already an act of dwelling. What was once ‘pure earth’ becomes, through repeated acts of care and repair, a lived territory. The plot carries the memory of that founding gesture and, with it, a moral claim to belonging. Here, building still follows dwelling. But, elsewhere, the order has shifted. If Heidegger diagnosed the instrumentalisation of building and dwelling under the technical paradigm, financialisation pushes that logic further still. Over recent decades, housing has been drawn into the circuits of global finance: mortgages are bundled and traded, developments structured as investment vehicles, entire neighbourhoods acquired as investment portfolios. The house becomes an asset. Even its earlier status as a means to dwelling fades. Whether it is inhabited becomes secondary, sometimes irrelevant. This is a further step of abstraction: the house is valued not for the life it hosts, but for the returns it promises.

A Greek temple on a rocky promontory doesn’t merely occupy a site; it gathers a world

The consequences are visible. Across the globe, millions struggle to secure stable housing while large numbers of dwellings stand empty or underused. In several metropolises, high-rise developments marketed to investors remain partially unlit; elsewhere, entire districts rise in anticipation of demand that never fully materialises. The paradox is stark: houses without people, and people without houses. In an age of industrialised real estate, financialised housing and ‘smart homes’ managed by algorithms, it may seem of little use to look instead toward the precarious self-built houses of the urban margins.

Yet in self-building we encounter, perhaps more clearly than elsewhere, a form of practical wisdom – one that embodies and enacts the art of dwelling in the world as humans. This does not imply any idealisation of the poverty that often, though not invariably, accompanies processes of residential self-construction. Yet within conditions of housing precariousness there persists an everyday proximity to finitude – an awareness of fragility and contingency that stands as the counterpart to the human capacity to build a world: to carve out, patiently and imperfectly, a partially domesticated realm in which one may be at home.

Self-construction serves as a reminder that any house, if it is truly to be lived as such, must in some sense be self-built. It must answer to a dwelling that precedes and exceeds it; it must sustain a life and secure, however provisionally, a place in the world. In The Origin of the Work of Art (1950), Heidegger asks what it means for something to be a ‘work’. He turns to the example of a Greek temple on a rocky promontory. The temple doesn’t merely occupy a site; it gathers a world. Birth and death, blessing and disaster, victory and defeat find their measure in its presence. To create a work, he suggests, is to set up a world – to bring earth into appearance and allow things to assume weight and distance within a shared horizon.

The maternal house is one of the places from which a world first opens, what Gaston Bachelard once called the heart of the world for each person. It is there that we learn to distinguish near and far, intimate and foreign, belonging and estrangement. Walls retain memory; unfinished rooms carry expectation. In Heidegger’s evocation of the Black Forest hut, the house is not simply one place among others, but the place from which places are articulated – where earth and sky, mortals and divinities are gathered into a lived order.

We spend our lives trying to make a home of the world. In this, we resemble Homer’s Odysseus: always on the way, exposed to contingency, yet oriented toward a place that might gather our wanderings into something like belonging. Ithaca is not only something left behind, a lost origin; it also lies ahead, as a horizon we must reclaim again and again. At the end of The Odyssey, Penelope, unable to recognise her husband in the aged stranger before her, proposes a test: have our marriage bed moved. It cannot be done, Odysseus replies, because he himself carved it from the trunk of a living olive tree rooted in the ground. The house was built around it. Penelope recognises him at once. What confirms his identity is not simply memory, but a shared act of making – earth worked into form, a dwelling raised around it, a life sedimented in wood and soil. The bed is rooted because it was made there; it binds land appropriated, craft undertaken and a bond forged over time.

This does not mean that only an immovable house can be a home. Many of us inhabit several dwellings over a lifetime; some are rented, others provisional, others left behind. Yet every house that becomes a home requires something akin to that rooted bed: an act of appropriation and recognition through which a portion of the world is made one’s own. Through such a gesture, even the most fragile dwelling can become the place where one learns to dwell.
