item.title: Where the earth meets the sky
item.dc:creator: Aeon Video
item.description:
After half a century in the making, an observatory in New Mexico lets viewers peer 13,000 years into the future and the past

- by Aeon Video

Watch on Aeon
item.content:encoded:
Star Axis is an artwork of extraordinary ambition. For half a century, the US land artist Charles Ross has been building this ‘granite pyramid’ in a remote stretch of desert in New Mexico. The structure’s decades in the making, however, are just a blink in the timescale it aims to capture. The unique observatory puts 26,000 years of celestial movement perspective, allowing viewers to visualise Polaris – our steady ‘North Star’ throughout human history – becoming unfixed in the night sky.

In Where the Earth Meets the Sky, the filmmaker Rafael Salazar Moreno captures this project on the precipice of completion, with Ross – who started sketching Star Axis in 1971, in his early 30s – now in his late 80s. Bridging timescales of its own, the short documentary includes archival footage from the late filmmaker Wendy Apple, who died in 2017 and never saw Ross’s sprawling vision, or her own film chronicling it, completed. With his treatment, Moreno builds something remarkable in its own right: the film grapples with grand, overlapping questions about the meaning of art and our connection to the Universe in just 24 minutes.

item.title: Mecca and the mall
item.dc:creator: Azania Imtiaz Patel
item.description:
In a bid for spiritual renewal, I made a pilgrimage to Islam’s holy city. Almost everything I expected to see was gone

- by Azania Imtiaz Patel

Read on Aeon
item.content:encoded:
Listen to this essay

20 minute listen

It is Ramadan, the holiest month of the Islamic calendar, and I am sitting in a rooftop café in Mecca, the holiest city of the religion. The sun has gone down, and an array of glittering shops and hotels lights up the urban expanse below me. At the heart of this ancient city, the foremost site of Muslim worship, guarded with fortress-like marble walls, is the Masjid al-haram complex – the largest mosque in the world. I’ve just completed my own pilgrimage to the holy site, and I’m struggling to name the discomfort that I am feeling.

There are few words to describe the whiplash of coming face to face with a Joe & The Juice, a Sephora and a plethora of other shops and hotels and Times Square-style billboards after going through one of the most spiritually charged experiences of my life. To find myself in what seemed just like any other petrodollar-fuelled Gulf port instead of a sanctified land was jarring. I felt robbed of the romanticism I had expected after a childhood built on admiration for religious lore and high-flown notions of a fantastical divine city.

I’d found myself in Mecca, trying to catch a break from the existential dread of my day-to-day life – the constant round of applying for jobs I didn’t really want because it wasn’t sustainable to write full-time, going on first date after first date, trying to find love on apps that were designed for failure, doomscrolling social media while caught in a dopamine trap, and staring at my laptop screen while waiting for some revelation to break through the fog in my mind and string itself into life-changing words. My 30s were closing in, and I felt the noose of squandered potential around my neck.

One of my most frequent prayers comes from a verse in the Quran that narrates Moses’ escape from Egypt: ‘Rabbi inni lima anzalta ilayya min khairin faqir’ (‘My Lord, indeed I am in absolute need of whatever good You send down’). I have always been comforted by the notion that a divine power was looking after me, that something out there existed beyond the constraints of time and space – omnipresent, omnipotent – and yet closer to me than my jugular vein, as my Holy Book would tell me.

My rationale for the trip was that this kind of spiritual sugar rush would allow me to find my footing in the secular world. My worshipful hope was that God would be impressed by my performed devotion, and divine intervention would set my worldly affairs straight. And though I felt a sense of renewed worship in making my pilgrimage, that break from the ordinary world never came.

Islam is not an ascetic faith: interestingly, it prohibits monasticism. However, the state of being a pilgrim is the closest that one comes to forsaking the material world. Before entering the boundaries of the Holy City, dressed in a swishing white abaya with a prayer book hung on a lanyard around my neck, I had committed to a state of heightened spiritual purity known as the ihram.

The word ihram has etymological roots in the word haraam, which means to forbid. It is the embodiment of additional, out-of-the-ordinary prohibitions. In this consecrated state, pilgrims are not allowed to have sexual relations or to hunt an animal or to change the state of their body: they cannot cut their nails or hair, for example, or perfume themselves. Men must cover themselves only with two pieces of unstitched cloth, while women must wear unadorned garments that leave their faces and hands visible. The purpose of the ihram is to equalise worshippers for the duration of their pilgrimage. As the anthropologists Victor Turner and Edith Turner described (albeit in the context of Christianity), pilgrims occupy a liminal, threshold state. They enter a state of structural betweenness, termed ‘communitas’, where they find themselves stripped of their social identities, and in a temporary state of spontaneous egalitarianism.

There are two kinds of pilgrimages in the faith, the umrah – which takes a few hours to complete and can be done at any time of the year, and the Hajj – which takes five days, and can be performed only in the Islamic month of Dhul-Hijjah. Both pilgrimages require the same conditions of ihram. I began my umrah with a short ride to the Mosque on a government-funded shuttle service, decorated with an electric ticker that said: ‘Welcome Guests of Ar Rahman’, that is, guests of the Most Merciful. Pilgrims are not guests of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, but of God, and therefore, on paper, both prince and pauper must be alike. When in communitas, this sentiment feels enacted.

It is hard to look away from the symbol of your faith made manifest before you

Some pilgrims prayed on the shuttle with prayer beads, others read out verses from the Quran apps on their phones. Others still had prayer books similar to mine. But as we got closer to the Great Mosque, we were let off the bus, and everyone’s rhythmic chanting came into unison in a single phrase, as pilgrims cried out to the skies ‘Labbaik Allahumma Labbaik’ (‘Oh, here I am, my Lord! I have answered your call!’) The fervent declaration continued as we joined the crowd of thousands making their way on foot into the heart of Masjid al-Haram.

The first thing you experience when you enter the Great Mosque of Mecca is the smell of oudh and rosewater engulfing you. A cultural belief among many Muslim communities is that whatever you pray for when you first glance upon the Kaaba – the black raw-silk-covered cuboid stone at the centre of the mosque – will be granted, so most pilgrims enter for the first time with their eyes firmly planted on the cool marble floor – or held tightly shut as they hold on to the person guiding them in. And when you do open your eyes, that initial glance is surreal; an ocean of pilgrims clad in white circumambulate the Kaaba, flocks of swallows flit against the skyline, and there are hundreds of things in the periphery of your sightlines to be distracted by – from the towering malls to surveillance drones and battalions of guards with puffed chests patrolling against miscreants. Yet, despite these competing spectacles, it is hard to look away from the symbol of your faith made manifest before you – more enormous than you imagined, impossibly still, magnetic.

The Kaaba is an epitomic example of what Mircea Eliade, a foundational historian of religions, described in The Sacred and the Profane (1957) as ‘axis mundi’, or the navel of the Earth, a centre from which the world is said to have emerged. In Islamic belief, Mecca is the mother city, the land from which the rest of the world rolled out. In the same theology, the Kaaba was the first building on Earth, established for the worship of God, before being lost in the flood of Noah and then rebuilt by Abraham and his son Ismael in its present form.

Since Muhammad’s conquest of Mecca in 630 CE, the Kaaba has oriented all aspects of Muslim life. Wherever they are in the world, Muslims perform their five daily prayers facing towards the Kaaba, and dead bodies are buried with their head oriented in the same direction. The complex built around it encompasses all of the sacred topography you must go through on your pilgrimage. You start with the circumambulation of the Kaaba, before praying adjacent to the Maqam-e-Ibrahim, a stone enclosed in glass, which is supposed to bear the footprints of Abraham. Then, you must cross the distance between the hills of Safa and Marwa seven times, a total of 3.15 km (1.96 miles). Once these obligatory rituals of the umrah (which take a few hours) have been completed, men shave their heads, while women cut an inch or two of their hair to exit the state of being a pilgrim.

For Eliade, the sacred space marks a break from the locus of mundane, profane life. It is an anchor emerging through divine revelation, from which believers orient themselves, allowing access to a more primordial state of being. In the state of ihraam – eyes upon the anchor that had shaped my worship – my experience was more metaphysical than embodied. In those moments, I occupied an imagined Mecca, the fabled city of prophets and angels, and of mothers striving to keep faith in the face of cruel oppression. I could almost see what had been here before, the ghosts of a nascent faith, taking its first shaky breaths, keeping step with the flesh-and-bone believers centuries away.

Accessing that spiritual world required me to suspend my disbelief – because, in 2026, even the Great Mosque is, like Mecca itself, very different from the one I had read about in prophetic traditions. In the past decade, the mosque has been subject to a massive expansion and renovation project. At a cost of nearly $26.6 billion, the Saudi government has rebuilt the complex, growing it from 414,000 square metres to 1.564 million square metres of space, in order to accommodate a growing number of pilgrims and to make the area more accessible. However, this has come at a great cost to the historicity of the space and, to an extent, to the otherworldliness that the line between sacred and profane demands.

Except for the Kaaba, all historically significant structures in the complex have been either modified or destroyed

Four floors of marble walkways now surround the Kaaba, allowing more people to circumambulate at once. The different floors are accessed through a network of escalators and ramps. The final walkway comes with tracks for golf carts – and, at the price of 300 Saudi riyals ($80), pilgrims can complete their rituals on wheels. Those on a budget, meanwhile, can spend half that amount to rent a wheelchair if they’re struggling with walking more than the 2.5 miles expected.

In her travelogue Pilgrimage to Mecca (1934), Lady Evelyn Cobbold, the first British female convert to make the Hajj, wrote:

Even the Ford Motor could not vulgarise the lovely moon-splashed desert, whose stillness was unbroken by a camel caravan we passed, silently treading its way Northward; mysterious phantoms of beasts and men of another world than ours – I inwardly prayed that the motor may never displace the camel.

I wonder what she would make of the carts zipping through the mosque itself today. The consequence of these efficiency-oriented measures is that, except for the Kaaba, all historically significant structures in the Mecca complex have been either modified or destroyed.

The path between the hills of Safa and Marwa, where Muslims believe that the Prophet’s wife Hagar foraged for water, before the spring of holy water, Zamzam, miraculously burst open, has now been flattened and reconstructed as a multistorey, air-conditioned enclosure. The structure that marked the well of holy water has also been demolished, with pilgrims now able to access the water only through taps and tanks. Canopies dedicated to influential classical scholars of Islam within the mosque complex have been dismantled, while neon lights have been installed to mark the point at which circumambulation is to begin.

As I went through the rituals, the chasm between the sacred space in my mind and the very real, remade-for-modern-convenience one I occupied provoked a kind of grief. I mourned that these weren’t the same floors the forebears of my faith had walked, nor were these the pillars they had leaned against. On one hand, that sense of communitas with the other pilgrims nourished my soul; on the other, I was palpably aware of how much of a disjuncture I was at with the past. When I completed my pilgrimage, I reached under the swathes of my hijab to snip off a few curls from my head with small metal scissors. Exiting the state of ihram and physically changed by my acts of worship, I was pushed into a painful awareness of the mundane, profane world. The disjuncture became significantly more pronounced when I stepped out of the mosque.

In Cobbold’s memoir, written less than a century ago, Mecca is the city without walls, protected by mountains, with Bedouin caravans selling wares to pilgrims staying in modest homestays and camping on the desert trail. That Mecca no longer exists either. The homestays are gone, and the hospitable locals of yore now live on the outskirts of the city – their neighbourhoods swallowed up by hotels and shopping complexes.

Some changes are unavoidable. When Muhammad performed his final pilgrimage in 632 CE, an estimated 30,000 followers accompanied him. When I performed my pilgrimage in February 2026, an estimated 1.68 million people from abroad had been granted pilgrimage permits for the month of Ramadan. These pilgrims need space not just to worship, but also to sleep and eat, and to do all that mortal bodies do – and so infrastructure should be built to support those needs.

However, the de-historicisation of Mecca has been a calculated, ideological project, with what would be considered protected monuments in any other part of the world decimated to build vanity projects. Saudi Arabia’s premier religious ideology – Wahhabism – is an 18th-century revivalist movement that espouses a literalist, strict interpretation of the Quran, and it has encouraged the tearing down of historical sites such as the houses of early Islamic figures, and the enshrined gravesites of the Prophet’s family, claiming that they’d invite idolatry otherwise. The refitting of Mecca is also deeply entwined with the rise of the petrodollar in the Kingdom, creating a tense intersection where ritual jostles with capitalism for space. As the writer and public intellectual Ziauddin Sardar puts it in The Sacred City (2014), the Kingdom has made a steel and glass heaven of consumerism in the name of extinguishing idol worship.

Where those before us battled drought and death to find God, we battle excess and the temptation of abundance

So, now, a Hilton Hotel stands where the house of Islam’s first Caliph, Abu Bakr, once stood. A nondescript library stands in place of the home in which Muhammad was born, while an 18th-century citadel was torn down to make way for the Makkah Clock Tower complex, a collection of seven buildings that are part mall, part hotel. The tallest of these buildings is a Big Ben-esque structure, sporting a giant clock dial that overlooks the Kaaba.

On the back of the oil economy, the Kingdom has exported its brand of Wahhabi Islam across the world. Traditional ways of believing have been homogenised, and a dogmatic, cookie-cutter version of the faith has been parcelled off. In return, the Global North has exported the phenomenon of placelessness to Saudi Arabia, whereby an influx of foreign brands has remade both the country’s high streets and consumer choices. The commercial onslaught, compounded by the active destruction of material history, gives the fringes of sacred space a particular tone. Irfan al-Alawi, a theologian and heritage preservation proponent, described this in The Guardian as the ‘Manhattanisation of Mecca’.

As I walked through the grey concrete streets and glass malls of Mecca, I wondered if devotion here would have meant more when the skyline was dotted with sandy hills, and there was nothing but the House of God as your harbour against the angry desert. I contemplated whether my return to a comfortable hotel bed, and not a flimsy tent, implied something lacking in my commitment to giving up the material. Or perhaps it is just that I am of this time, and my prayers are subject to its whims. Indeed, perhaps it is in that very unease that ritual finds meaning – if all the world were holy, we would not gravitate as we do to the omphalos (literally, ‘navel’). The sacred is significant because it disrupts the profane. Where those before us battled drought and death to find God, we must battle excess and the temptation of abundance.

I can’t presume to know what God thinks of today’s Mecca. After all, to evolve is natural to the holy city; it has been moulded to dynasties and clerical moods over centuries. Belief continues to move past anachronisms, and yet, as one prays by the black-and-gold cloth-covered Kaaba, the shadow of the clock towers falls upon you – a too-obvious metaphor in action.

item.title: Bouncy brothers
item.dc:creator: Aeon Video
item.description:
Two brothers struggle to keep a bouncy house business afloat in this nuanced portrait of family and the pursuit of success

- by Aeon Video

Watch on Aeon
item.content:encoded:
For his celebrated short documentary Bouncy Brothers, the US director Nicholas J Santore chronicled his uncle Anthony Glazier’s pursuit of the American dream – that deeply entrenched national notion that anyone with a worthy idea and sweat to spare can succeed. Attempting to escape the confines of suburban Chicago and the nine-to-five grind, Glazier upended his life in his 50s, moving away from his extended family to run an inflatable bouncy house business in central Florida.

Santore’s film captures Glazier’s hopes for self-sufficiency colliding with harsh realities. Unreliable help, fickle clients, thin margins and his easy-going personality make it difficult to turn a profit despite his dedication to making it work. With his business barely staying aloft, his brother Ted moves to Florida for the summer to try to help him save it. Framed by intimate cinematography and Santore’s connection with his subjects, what emerges is a nuanced portrait of brotherhood that subtly challenges what it means to succeed in a capitalist system.

item.title: A second sexual revolution
item.dc:creator: Rosa Campbell
item.description:
Until Shere Hite’s Report, even the most daring sexologists refused to listen to what women desired and hated in sex

- by Rosa Campbell

Read on Aeon
item.content:encoded:
Listen to this essay

28 minute listen

In 1972, Shere Hite, a Playboy model turned feminist sex researcher, jumped on a motorbike and drove around Manhattan. With a cascade of strawberry blonde curls peeping out under the helmet, rosebud lips visible under the visor, and a vintage lace gown streaming behind her, she handed out surveys to any woman who would take one. It was all about sex. Across 58 questions, Hite asked: ‘Could you describe what an orgasm feels like to you?’; ‘Do you feel free to do all the things you would like [in sex], or do you think the other person(s) would be shocked?’; ‘Do you think sex is in any way political?’ The responses formed the basis of the feminist sexology bestseller The Hite Report: A Nationwide Study of Female Sexuality (1976). It sold 50 million copies.

This was among the first books that asked women how they felt about sex, rather than telling them what to feel. Its great provocation was that most American women were sexually dissatisfied: 70 per cent of them could not orgasm from penetrative sex but required clitoral stimulation; a significant proportion of women faked orgasms. The Hite Report remains the 30th bestselling book of all time, and one of the most-read books of the 20th century. Yet today it and its author have largely vanished.

By the early 1970s, the number of young women in the US who reported having had premarital sex was around 62 per cent – up from 7.6 per cent of those born before 1900. The Pill was widely available – 10 million women were using it – decoupling sex from reproduction for the first time in history. And the introduction of no-fault divorce in California in 1969 (soon followed by other states) meant that women could more easily free themselves from loveless marriages. Into this confounding sexual revolution Shere published her Hite Report.

Hite found that the sexual revolution meant more sex for women, but not better sex. For many of the women she surveyed, sex still followed a similar and unsatisfactory pattern that one woman described as ‘a little kiss, a little feel, a finger for arousal, a touch of breast and he’s on top, wham it’s over.’ Invariably, male orgasm determined the end of sex. One woman, freed up by the sexual revolution to have many lovers, noted that ‘I’m beginning to think there must be something like a sexual “Robert’s Rules of Order” which every guy follows.’ Even Alex Comfort’s widely read book The Joy of Sex (1972) couldn’t get away from the sexual script that saw penis-in-vagina sex as the pièce de résistance. (A Black lesbian who filled out the Original Survey, on which The Hite Report was based, remarked that she ‘didn’t think much’ of Comfort’s contribution.) Women also felt that during the sexual revolution they had ‘lost their right to say “no”’. One woman told Hite: ‘Most men didn’t give a damn about whether I wanted to have sex with them or not; if I didn’t want to screw them, they would … try to lecture me into being “free”.’ Sexual inequality percolated through the revolution.

Hite’s path to feminism was unusual. While enrolled on a PhD at Columbia University in New York, she worked as a model, sometimes doing fashion jobs, sometimes porn (which paid better), and was hired by Olivetti typewriters to appear in an advertisement. But, as Hite later recalled, when the advertisement was published, she found her image appeared beneath a sexist caption: ‘The typewriter is so smart that she doesn’t have to be.’ That prompted the New York chapter of the National Organization for Women (NOW) to launch a protest. They marched through Manhattan with placards that proclaimed ‘Don’t Drown In The Olivetti Typing Pool’. Hite was overjoyed by the support. She contacted NOW and soon became involved in political campaigns and consciousness-raising groups (CR), the key tactic of women’s liberation.

At CR, women met in small groups to talk about how a sexist society shaped them, often against their own interests. They would take turns answering questions like ‘How do you feel about housework?’ and ‘How do you feel about ageing?’ Women came to understand that their feelings – often bad – were political, the result of a deeply unequal world, not their individual failings. They often described this moment of consciousness raising as a ‘click’: there was a political cause to their personal misery. Feelings were a form of expertise. Women could follow them to paint a collective picture of what life was like as women, what needed to change, and how they might go about it. But Hite noticed something else at CR. Women talked of their feelings about every aspect of culture and society – except for sex. Even in these groups, sex was still considered a private matter – personal, even shameful.

A porn mag ran Hite’s questionnaire ‘in the interest of better communication [with] women’

There had been some feminist writing about sex. In The Myth of the Vaginal Orgasm (1970), Anne Koedt argued forcefully that all orgasms were clitoral. Erica Jong, in her novel Fear of Flying (1973), celebrated the pleasures of the ‘zipless fuck’ (a sexual encounter without commitment or emotion). Nancy Friday’s My Secret Garden (1973) detailed women’s most explicit fantasies. Both Friday’s and Jong’s works were blockbusters, and many women who filled out Hite’s Original Survey reported reading them. But how did these declarations, fictitious accounts and wild wishes match up to the truth of women’s sex lives? To find out, Hite proposed a weekend-long CR conference to discuss sex, frankly. Her comrades, however, were flabbergasted, even horrified; one woman protested: ‘You think I’m going to stand up and tell everyone about how I have orgasms!’ To overcome women’s shyness and shame about sex, Hite developed her anonymous questionnaire.

Hite’s questionnaire travelled well beyond the women’s movement. First, she handed it out in New York, and soon she was sending 100,000 copies through abortion rights groups and church newsletters. Brides and Mademoiselle magazines reproduced the questionnaire, and Oui, a porn mag, ran it ‘in the interest of better communication [with] women’, alongside a centrefold of ‘better girls than last month’. Men passed it to their wives and girlfriends, and women who came across the questionnaire showed it wide-eyed to their female friends, mothers passed it to sisters, and teachers to students.

Responses to the questionnaire uncovered something surprising. The major influence on many women’s sex lives was not feminism or the sexual revolution, but psychoanalysis. In Sigmund Freud’s Three Essays on the Theory of Sexuality (1905), he grafted ideas of mature/immature and healthy/dysfunctional forms of female sexuality onto the vagina and clitoris, respectively. According to Freud, girls find pleasure in their clitoris, just as young boys do in their penis, but as girls mature into women, the pleasure centre moves from the clitoris to the vagina as women ‘put aside their childish masculinity’. In the mature, heterosexual woman, Freud located the erotic and the reproductive in the same place: the vagina.

As Freud saw it, the clitoris would naturally ‘transmit excitation to the adjacent sexual parts’ the way a ‘pine shaving’ would help ‘set a log of harder wood on fire’. The ‘log’ he was referring to was the vagina – but this simile choice was a monstrous Freudian slip, exposing who the vaginal orgasm was for, whose pleasure it would increase, and the limits of Freud’s own gender politics. If grown women could not orgasm vaginally because the ‘vaginal orifice’ remained ‘anaesthet[ised]’, this was because of their sexual immaturity. Freud recommended this should be treated with psychoanalysis. In other words, not being able to orgasm vaginally was seen as a mental illness.

By the 1970s, the problem was with conservative neo-Freudians. Many women who could not orgasm vaginally had been sent to Freudian psychotherapy, which wholly embraced anti-feminism from the 1940s on. As the historian Jane Gerhard has shown in Desiring Revolution (2001), psychoanalysts held that heterosexual, reproductive sex was the only model of ‘mature’ femininity. In therapy, women were told that their lack of vaginal orgasm was a result of neurotic blocks and deficiencies in the psyche, and they believed it. One woman told Hite: ‘I can have an orgasm with clitoral stimulation but I have never had one with intercourse. This is purely a fear thing … My therapist helped me see it.’ Another spoke of how she came to see clitoral orgasm as ‘selfish or infantile (thanks to Freud, I guess).’

Conservative neo-Freudians insisted to women that their inability to orgasm vaginally was a physical symptom of their psychic refusal to adjust to their role as women. This was the price they paid for rejecting their passive, maternal place in the bedroom and the family. The idea extended far beyond the therapist’s office. Even if women were not in therapy, Hite, like Betty Friedan before her, suggested that the ‘influence of these psychiatric theories on women has been strong and pervasive … these unfounded and anti-women theories [are] endlessly repeated’ in women’s magazines, in movies, in marriage manuals. In the survey, women used therapeutic language again and again to scold themselves: ‘I must let go, relax and trust, unlearn my taboos and defences.’

This is why major feminist thinkers like Hite, Friedan, Shulamith Firestone and Kate Millett wrote against psychoanalysis. As they saw it, therapy helped women to accept the unacceptable and adjust to the conditions around them, rather than changing those conditions. ‘I wish we could have back all the time and energy we have spent blaming ourselves,’ Hite wrote. ‘And all the money we have spent “flocking to the psychiatrists” … I would like to have what we would have built with that energy.’

By looking at sex through the lens of feminism, Hite found that it was shot through with power and inequality

In her questionnaire, she also asked about recent sexology: ‘Have you read Masters and Johnson’s recent scientific studies on human sexual response …? What did you think of them? Of Kinsey? Any other writers?’ She wondered if this newer work would help women flip the sexual script. Working across the 1940s and ’50s, the biologist Alfred Kinsey was interested in how people really did it, beyond what social norms prescribed. Through in-depth interviews with 18,000 people, he sought to learn how people had sex, with whom, and how often. He fearlessly asked: did people have sex outside marriage? With people of the same sex? In public? With animals? He published his Kinsey Reports in 1948 (on men) and 1953 (on women), after which The Hite Report was named. As Hite explained on The Mike Douglas Show in 1982: ‘Kinsey did a service in putting on the map how often people did what with whom. But my area was a little different, I asked people Why do you do it?, How do you feel about it? And Would you like to be different? Would you like things to be different? So I’m really trying to draw a larger picture of the society and how people are feeling within that society.’

The gynaecologist William Masters and the sexologist Virginia Johnson were interested in people’s physical responses to sex. They conducted direct laboratory observation of nearly 10,000 sex acts from the late 1950s to 1965. They invited volunteers – initially sex workers – and hooked them up to wires, which enabled them to measure heart rate during sex and contractions during orgasm. They observed women having sex with a glass dildo improbably called Ulysses. A light and camera within Ulysses allowed them to see inside the vagina during sex, and observe the moment of orgasm. This led to the conclusion, important for The Hite Report, that all women’s orgasms were clitoral orgasms, and that women who were orgasming from intercourse were doing so because the clitoris was indirectly stimulated by the penis. Masters and Johnson’s findings gave them the opportunity to depose penetration as the highest form of sex – and elevate masturbation, clitoral stimulation and lesbian sex as possibilities. Alas, they did not. Instead, they merely suggested that most women could orgasm from the indirect stimulation of the clitoris during penetration, that this was automatic, part of the ‘normal’ course of sex.

Hite concluded that Masters and Johnson never suggested direct clitoral stimulation for women because ‘they continued to view sex through certain cultural blinders’. She was being diplomatic here; these two researchers were deeply committed to monogamous, heterosexual marriage as the highest form of relationship. From 1968, they ran a treatment programme for ‘dissatisfied homosexual men’, helping them to ‘convert’ to heterosexuality, which continued long after homosexuality was removed from the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders as a psychological disorder in 1973. Masters and Johnson’s ideas about women also reflected the pair’s sexual values. If orgasm for women was par for the course, this meant that there was no need for men to have sex differently; they could maintain the predictable sex that served them so well and many women not at all.

For Hite, it wasn’t because of lack of knowledge that women didn’t speak up about what they wanted in sex – it was lack of power. Her great innovation lay in bringing feminism to sex. By looking at sex through the lens of feminism, Hite found that it was shot through with power and inequality. Society insisted that women, like men, should find their greatest pleasure in penetrative sex: the woman penetrated, the man penetrating. In an interview in 1977, Hite declared that ‘sex is sexist … women’s sex lives clearly reflect their second-class position in the society. Women, still, in 1976, make only 60 per cent of the amount of money men make for the same work: men have the right to more rewards (money, services, respect) than women. Just so in sex.’

Like many white women involved in the women’s liberation movement, Hite understood gender as the primary oppression in women’s lives, from which all other oppression, such as class and race, flowed. Black feminists argued that when the women’s movement referred to women it meant white women, but this whiteness was almost never mentioned – it was made invisible in the universal idea of ‘woman’.

Race went unanalysed in Hite’s study. But Black women did read and respond. They filled out her questionnaire and wrote letters after they read the book, and often they pushed her project further. One Black woman, who recorded her responses on tape, remarked: ‘When I was growing up, Black women had no beauty.’ A young Black law student wrote that she couldn’t ‘screw across barriers’, that white men didn’t desire her. A Chinese American woman noted that her racial identity made a difference to her sex life. She noted sardonically that ‘Chinese is “in” this year.’ These responses demonstrated how race and racism are, like gender injustice, woven into sexual encounters, and offer insight into how women of colour negotiated this discrimination.

What has become of the sexual revolution – and what does Hite’s work still have to offer? Today, women’s pleasure is taken more seriously – thanks, in part, to feminists like Hite. The majority of women whom Hite surveyed regularly masturbated to orgasm, but felt ‘lonely, guilty, unwanted, selfish, silly and generally bad’ as a result. That shame is not nearly as widespread as it used to be: one study of American women in 2014 found that a majority felt ‘sexually empowered’ after masturbating. In the UK, the Labour MP Samantha Niblett launched ‘Yes Sex Please, We’re British!’, a play on the title of a comedy film from 1973; she plans to host a sex-toy exhibition in the Palace of Westminster as part of her campaign to promote sex education and destigmatise women’s pleasure.

Laws around rape and consent have changed too, owing to feminist pressure. As legal scholars and historians such as Alecia Simmonds, Izabella Scott and Joanna Bourke write, rape is no longer a crime of force as it was in previous centuries – defined as damage to a man’s property, that is, his wife or virgin daughter. Rape has been redefined in terms of sexual consent. Courts in rape trials now ascertain how consent was given or not: what did the victim say, what did the perpetrator ask? And consent has permeated sexual politics far beyond the courts. It’s not just the litmus test for whether sex was rape, but the mode by which pleasurable sex can be achieved. We are, as the scholar Katherine Angel writes in Tomorrow Sex Will Be Good Again (2021), living in an age where ‘the ideal … of consent reigns supreme.’

Since the 2000s, women have been urged to find out what they want and go for it assertively. The rise of consent politics dovetailed with the age of ‘girl boss’ feminism, which urged women to ‘lean in’ in both their personal and professional lives. Hite helped usher in this change. In her book she urged women: ‘You have to care about yourself and want to please yourself, and you have to feel it is your right. You have to do it, whatever it is – or ask for it, very clearly and very specifically.’

Hite was highly combative, quick to quit interviews if she sensed misogyny (which was often)

And yet, for Hite, knowing yourself and speaking up was only the beginning. It was not a bad start, but she knew that structural inequality couldn’t really be solved by a straight couple in bed, no matter how honest their communication. She knew that inequality pervades our choices and feelings long before we’ve set foot in the bedroom, before we’ve uttered a yes or a no.

The focus today on consent has not challenged gender inequality beyond the bedroom. The gender pay gap, attacks on abortion rights, endemic sexual violence, and the orgasm gap – which names the disparity between men and women’s orgasms in straight sex – roll on relentlessly, shaping our desires long before the sexual encounter. Nor has our age of consent held back the tide of the alt-Right. Manosphere influencers preach that women’s sexual assertiveness is evidence that feminism has gone too far and that the world is now stacked against men. Tradwives, too, argue that women having multiple sexual partners (which they refer to as a ‘body count’) before marriage makes them unhappy, resorting to tired old claims that women are not ‘built’ for casual sex – only monogamy, childbearing and wifely submission.

Hite published two more books: The Hite Report on Male Sexuality (1981) and Women and Love (1987). The responses to these were very different from her first. The later books were methodologically flawed, and the statistics she uncovered were startling to the point of being unconvincing: ‘84 per cent of women are not satisfied emotionally with their relationships,’ she claimed, and 70 per cent of women and men in long-term marriages had affairs. These statistics were not corroborated; other research reported an infidelity rate of 15-20 per cent for women. Furthermore, Hite was highly combative, quick to quit interviews if she sensed misogyny (which was often). She herself became the story – not the inarguable data of a robust survey. When in 1987 an interviewer for the TV show 60 Minutes Australia opened with: ‘You’ve been accused of man bashing –’ Hite interrupted him to say: ‘Yeah, and it’s gonna happen right here!’ before storming out. The media had their narrative, and it wasn’t her serious work.

During the anti-feminist backlash of the late-1980s and ’90s, Hite disappeared in a storm of media attacks, wrought by a rising New Right. Many conservatives felt that the upheavals of the 1960s – feminism and civil rights – had shattered their worlds. The New Right, which included Evangelical leaders such as Tim LaHaye and Jerry Falwell, and Right-wing women such as Phyllis Schlafly, Anita Bryant and Beverly LaHaye, gave vent to this gathering discontent. They argued that feminism was ‘unnatural’ and that biological differences between men and women excused inequality. They braided this with a politics of grievance, suggesting that the progressive politics of the 1960s and ’70s had captured the interests of government and left ‘ordinary’ Americans behind.

Soon, the media closed ranks. From the London Review of Books and The Washington Post to the New York Post and Penthouse, all went after her. Time magazine wrote that Women and Love was ‘the author’s own male-bashing diatribe’, and that the entire book was ‘full of extreme views’ of malcontented women. New York magazine claimed that she ‘totally neglects biology’, and that men were naturally promiscuous. If the success of the first Hite Report narrates the rise of feminism, then the later trashing of Hite tells the story of its conservative backlash. Hite fled the US in the mid-1990s, and spent her last years living peripatetically across Europe. She died in Tottenham, north London, in 2020.

In the first Hite Report she quoted several women on how the women’s movement changed their sex lives. One wrote: ‘With the onset of the women’s movement, and its personal effect on me, I’ve stopped faking them.’ Another: ‘I don’t think I ever asked for what I wanted … Now the women’s movement has helped me to be outspoken. I ask for what I want in all sorts of situations – church, work, the supermarket, local government – and in bed.’ It was women’s liberation that would make ‘a new kind of physical relations to go with a new, more humane and pro-women society’. In the long term, a gender-just world would remake the conditions that shaped desires and change the way that sexual choices are moulded. But Hite believed that feminist struggle would change women in the present, too. As women came to see themselves and others not as objects but as subjects, they would begin, at last, to be free. Throughout her life, Hite was uncompromising: to change sex for the better, women must be feminists.

item.description:
The oldest Buddhist temple in Europe is an architectural anomaly, built in memory of the Kalmyk regiment that fought Napoleon

- by Aeon Video

Watch on Aeon
item.content:encoded: This video essay from the YouTube channel Kings and Things explores the intricate history and unique architecture of what’s widely considered to be the oldest surviving Buddhist temple in Europe: Khosheutovsky khurul in southwestern Russia. With rich archival imagery, the video traces its founding as a memorial to members of a Kalmyk regiment that fought Napoleon’s army, through its shuttering following the Russian Revolution, to its reopening and continued use today – albeit in a significantly modified form. From the story of this single structure emerges a brief introduction to the Kalmyk people and a unique perspective on two centuries of Russian history.

item.title: How we meet the future
item.dc:creator: Tom Ralston
item.description:
If we couldn’t make generalisations, we would be paralysed by the world’s complexity. Does that ever excuse stereotyping?

- by Tom Ralston

Read on Aeon
item.content:encoded:
Listen to this essay

23 minute listen

Overgeneralising has a bad rap. It seems an obvious, if understandable, mistake to generalise beyond what our evidence supports. A child playing in the park may assume, based on their experiences of their friendly pet golden retriever, that all dogs are friendly. But they would be wrong to approach an XL Bully, a breed of dog effectively outlawed in the UK recently following a string of attacks on children. When someone makes unwarranted generalisations about social groups, we condemn them for the sin of stereotyping. It is wrong to conclude after just one experience with a rude Brit that all Brits are rude.

We hear less about the problems of undergeneralising. Generalising comes so naturally that few of us are at any risk of undergeneralising, so we give it little thought. The focus on overgeneralising is understandable given its potential costs, such as the child assuming that a dangerous dog is just like the friendly dogs they’ve encountered to date. Generalising itself, though, isn’t a bias that needs to be corrected. It is a cognitive shortcut and a fundamental part of our mental life. We’d be lost without it. It gives our experience structure and frees us up to focus on the new at the expense of the old. The child who approaches the XL Bully and the person who stereotypes Brits risk making a mistake, but the source of their error is not their desire to generalise.

What, then, is wrong with overgeneralising?

Our story begins in Cambridge, 1930. Searching through the papers of his recently deceased friend, the philosopher Richard Braithwaite discovered a sheaf of handwritten notes on the nature of general beliefs, such as the belief that all humans are mortal. The friend was Frank Plumpton Ramsey, the remarkable philosopher and mathematician described as a ‘genius by all tests for genius’ by Paul Samuelson, the Nobel Laureate in economics. The notes were written in September 1929, just four months before Ramsey’s death from a mysterious illness that he may have contracted from swimming in the River Cam. Ramsey died aged just 26 but would go on to leave an oversized legacy in philosophy, mathematics, economics and logic.

In those notes, later titled ‘General Propositions and Causality’ by Braithwaite, Ramsey advocated a view of generalisations that renounced both his own previous views and those of Ludwig Wittgenstein, on whom the young Ramsey, until only recently an undergraduate, exerted a significant influence during their time together in Cambridge in the late 1920s.

Ramsey wanted to know what it means to say that a person believes that all humans are mortal. He concluded that, if you believe a generalisation, you have a habit or disposition. If you believe that all humans are mortal, you will take care not to run over your friends with your car and to make sure they have air to breathe, because you are disposed to treat any human you meet as mortal. Together, these habits and dispositions make up the system with which we ‘meet the future’. They are how we orient ourselves in the face of new observations and experiences.

Two people can disagree in their beliefs about generalisations, even when they agree on all the facts about particulars

What is the alternative? Wittgenstein, with whose writing Ramsey was very familiar, having worked on the translation of the fiendishly cryptic Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus (1921) from German into English while still an undergraduate, had argued that to believe a generalisation is to believe an infinite conjunction of facts about particulars: Alan is mortal and Bella is mortal and Carl is mortal and so on for every human being you could possibly mention. Ramsey’s new view saw beliefs in generalisations as involving a disposition to treat any human you encounter as mortal. That’s a bit different. After all, the disposition is a good one to the extent that it gets things right when tested. The disposition to treat any human I meet as mortal has not led me astray so far, but the disposition to treat any human as having blonde hair would falter quickly. That is why I don’t believe that all humans have blonde hair.

Why did Ramsey reject his earlier view? Ramsey saw that two people can disagree in their beliefs about generalisations, even when they agree on all the facts about particulars. Imagine that I am debating a techno-utopian who believes that mortality is only a contingent feature of humanity’s present existence and that, in principle, humans could live forever. I can agree with them that every human up to now has been mortal, but at the same time disagree over the question of whether all humans are mortal. The techno-utopian would disagree with me that all humans are mortal, even though no human has yet achieved immortality. If believing the generalisation involved believing only that each previous human had been mortal, we could not disagree without disagreeing about a particular human’s mortality. But we agree about all past humans having been mortal. That’s not contested. We disagree only about possible future humans, without disagreeing about any particular human. My disposition to treat humans as mortal would come unstuck in a possible future in which some tech wizard unlocks the secret of immortality. Our disagreement does not concern the facts about the mortality of any actual human, but rather the possible future applications of the disposition.

This new perspective helps to explain why Ramsey revised his earlier view of generalisations. Rather than asking What does the world need to be like for a belief in a generalisation to be true?, Ramsey asked What is a belief in a generalisation for? His answer, as I’ve already suggested, is: to meet the future. Why? Human experience is far too complex for us to attend to every detail. We must be selective in the things we pay attention to. But how do we decide what to focus on and what to ignore? Beliefs in generalisations help to solve this dilemma. When I see a double-decker red vehicle in London, I can use my general knowledge about buses to predict that it is going to pull in at the next bus stop to pick up the person signalling with their arm. I don’t have to wait to see what the vehicle does, which frees me up to focus my attention elsewhere. These predictions don’t need to be infallible to be useful. When a bus is full or off duty, it won’t stop for passengers. Even if my beliefs sometimes lead me to make a mistake, I use them in generalisations to make predictions about what the future will be like, and I use these predictions to decide what to ignore.

Not all our generalisations are put to the same use. For Ramsey, whether we should believe a generalisation depends on the virtues of the habit that constitutes the belief. Universal generalisations admit no exceptions: upon meeting a single hairless Sphynx cat, I should no longer believe that all cats are furry. This feature of universal generalisations means that, if they are to be useful, they must be formulated with a high degree of precision. My belief that all cats are furry is too coarse-grained. I should perhaps have believed that all cats except Sphynx cats are furry instead. But even that won’t be quite right, once I learn about Ukrainian Levkoys. And, as they become more precise, these beliefs become less useful, because they become more complex, with too many ad hoc clauses. We go from the simple ‘All cats are furry’ to ‘All cats except Sphynx cats and Ukrainian Levkoys and this one and that one… are furry.’

Ramsey, a mathematically inclined philosopher, was interested in precisely formulated universal generalisations. But many of the generalisations that we believe don’t demand this kind of precision. I believe that cats are furry. How many hairless cats do I have to meet before I should abandon this belief? Generalisations like ‘Cats are furry’, without a quantifying word such as ‘all’ or ‘most’, are now known to philosophers and linguists as generic generalisations. They are about what is generally true of a category (cats), but do not say what proportion of the category has the property in question (being furry). I can answer the question How many cats are furry? by saying Most cats are furry, but not just Cats are furry. These are more common in everyday life than the universal generalisations that philosophers and logicians like to deal with.

My disposition to treat any cat as furry can lead me to error, but it gets things right enough of the time

As with the universal generalisations Ramsey discussed, to believe a generic generalisation is to be disposed to treat members of a category as having some property. Where they differ is that generic beliefs need not be revised in the face of one or even many counterexamples. I can hold on to my belief that cats are furry in the knowledge that many cats have no fur at all. I don’t need to revise my belief that buses pull in to pick up passengers just because they don’t when they are full. Things can get even more extreme: as the philosopher and cognitive scientist Sarah-Jane Leslie has argued, people will accept that mosquitoes carry the West Nile virus even when they are aware that only 1 per cent of mosquitoes are carriers. Sometimes, an incredibly strong correlation is not enough to warrant a belief in a generic generalisation: I don’t believe that humans are right-handed, even though around 90 per cent of us are.

All of this makes it extremely difficult to answer the question: what does the world need to be like for a generic generalisation to be true? Taking inspiration from Ramsey, we can ask instead: what are generic generalisations for? They are generalisations about a category, but they don’t apply univocally to every member of the category. Because they are tolerant of exceptions, they demand less of us than universal generalisations do. They don’t require us to revise our beliefs in the face of counterexamples. This surprising and rarely mentioned feature is what makes them so useful: I can form many generic beliefs about categories without worrying about getting things precisely right in every case. My disposition to treat any cat I meet as furry will sometimes lead me to error, but it is still worth holding on to that disposition because it gets things right enough of the time. And when I get things wrong, it is unlikely that there will be much of a cost. Before encountering it, I might mistakenly assume that my friend’s new cat will be furry and then discover that it is a Sphynx cat, but errors of this kind are not going to keep me up at night.

So far, so good for generic generalisations. They simplify the world by abstracting away from individual differences. They are insensitive to proportions, so we don’t need precise statistical evidence to support them. They admit exceptions so we don’t continually need to revise them. But the very features that make generic generalisations so useful are also hallmarks of stereotypes. Universal generalisations don’t make for good stereotypes – they are too easy to falsify by finding a single counterexample. Generic generalisations are better suited to this task, since we can hold on to them even when we know of a large number of counterexamples.

To stereotype a category is to associate certain properties with the category and its members. Like other beliefs in generalisations, stereotypes are part of the system with which we meet the future. They impose structure on our experiences. We cannot attend to every individual difference but instead use these beliefs to simplify our experience and make predictions about the future. And we do not revise our beliefs in these generalisations every time we meet an exception, for fear of abandoning the structure they provide.

Stereotyping social groups, including those defined by nationality, gender or skin colour, is typically thought morally wrong, because it undermines people’s autonomy by focusing on their membership of a group, rather than their qualities as individuals. It is common to hear that stereotyping is not only a moral failing, but an epistemic one, a failure of rationality or to fulfil our duties as knowers. We are sometimes even told that a tendency to stereotype is a consequence of low cognitive ability.

There are many ways that stereotyping might contribute to an epistemic failure. It often leads us to error, in part because the evidence from which we generalise is bad. Stereotypical portrayals of members of historically oppressed ethnic groups in film and television can form the basis for stereotypical generalisations about those groups, which in turn perpetuate the stereotype in future portrayals. Stereotyping might cause us to systematically misinterpret ambiguous evidence in a way that leads us to develop pernicious false beliefs. Black people in the UK are significantly more likely to be stopped and searched by police officers than white people. Holding a racial stereotype about that group might lead a person to conclude incorrectly that its members have a higher innate propensity to commit crimes.

Generalising means meeting the future with assumptions that make the world around us intelligible

Important though these troubling aspects of stereotyping are, I am more interested in the question of whether there is something inherently irrational in the epistemic attitude that leads to stereotyping.

To answer that question, we must consider why we stereotype at all. Stereotyping is a form of generalising. People stereotype because they need to simplify their experience. And because we all need to simplify our experience, we should not rule out stereotyping as inherently irrational. It may often lead us to error, but our mistake is not our desire to generalise.

Human cognition is limited. That is why mental shortcuts like generalising are an essential part of our mental lives. In Daniel Kahneman’s 2002 Nobel Prize-winning work on bounded rationality, summarised in his Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011) and originally developed with Amos Tversky, he found that people employ a range of cognitive heuristics when asked to make complex judgments. Heuristics are ways of making decisions under conditions of uncertainty or limited resources. Because they allow us to ignore a lot of information, heuristics are not always accurate. In a 1983 study by Kahneman and Tversky illustrating the ‘conjunction fallacy’, people were presented with the following vignette:

Linda is 31 years old, single, outspoken and very bright. She majored in philosophy. As a student, she was deeply concerned with issues of discrimination and social justice, and also participated in anti-nuclear demonstrations.

Their participants, including those with sophisticated knowledge of statistics, judged ‘Linda is a bank teller and is active in the feminist movement’ to be more probable than ‘Linda is a bank teller’, given the information in the vignette. But the former entails the latter and so cannot be more probable. Instead of applying precise statistical reasoning, people are employing a ‘representativeness’ heuristic, where the first option is judged more probable than the second because the description of Linda is more representative of their idea of a feminist bank teller than of a bank teller. It is tempting to interpret this as evidence of widespread irrationality, but to dismiss these heuristics out of hand is to ignore the value of such cognitive shortcuts. We often need to reason quickly or with only partial evidence, and heuristics are invaluable in such circumstances. A person who never employed heuristic thinking would be overwhelmed by competing cognitive demands. Heuristics, though fallible in systematic ways, are essential tools for navigating the complexity of experience.

Generalising is another kind of cognitive shortcut. Like Tversky and Kahneman’s heuristics, it may lead us to errors. This is because generalising inherently goes beyond our evidence. My dispute with the techno-utopian over the mortality of humans concerns what is possible for humans; we don’t disagree about the evidence that is available.

Generalising means meeting the future with assumptions that make the world around us intelligible, but at the expense of paying less attention to individual differences. Stereotyping is a way of making the social world intelligible. That does not make stereotyping right. It can be accurate or wildly inaccurate, and it lends itself to abuse. It can harm members of stereotyped groups in many ways, in part because it is a failure to see people as individuals, rather than simply as members of a category. The cognitive utility of stereotyping does not make it rational: holding on to a stereotype in the face of overwhelming evidence against it is surely irrational. But it does make stereotyping understandable and perhaps even morally excusable, since it reflects our need to make predictions about the future, based on the categories that things, including people, fall into.

How do we find a balance between undergeneralising and overgeneralising? One place to start is to seek out counterexamples to our generalisations. We can then rule out at least some of our general beliefs as false. This response to the problem of generalisations was proposed by the philosopher of science Karl Popper. He famously argued that, strictly speaking, we are never justified in believing that universal generalisations are true on the basis of experience, since there is always another potential counterexample lurking beyond our observation. We are, however, justified in believing that a universal generalisation is false when we know of a single counterexample. A single immortal human would falsify the generalisation that all humans are mortal.

This proposal works well enough for universal generalisations, since we can easily state the conditions in which they are false. Popper’s concern was the practice of science, where the precision of universal generalisations is welcome. But many of our everyday general beliefs are not beliefs in universal generalisations. They are, instead, generic beliefs. The problem with these beliefs is that neither ordinary speakers nor trained linguists have a clear idea of the conditions under which generic generalisations are true or false. They are tolerant of exceptions, so the mere fact that there are some hairless cats does not mean my belief that cats are furry is false. And if we can’t say when they are false, then Popper’s suggested search for counterevidence will not tell us what (not) to believe.

Without clear criteria for truth and falsity, how can we say what evidence should lead us to revise our generic beliefs? Here’s my answer. We should, like Ramsey, approach this question pragmatically. There are two factors that we should take into account when evaluating our generic beliefs. Both rest on Ramsey’s idea that beliefs in generalisations are dispositions to be judged by their consequences. For any particular generic generalisation we should ask two questions. First, how often does it lead us into error? Second, how costly are the consequences of these errors? Our replies will not give us a definitive answer, as Popper hoped, to the question of whether we should revise our beliefs in generalisations. But, if we follow Popper’s advice and actively seek out counterexamples, and try to falsify them to test their strength, then they can act as a guide, helping us to weigh up the importance of getting things right and the consequences of getting things wrong.

My generic beliefs about social categories need to meet a higher standard than those about mosquitoes

If I believe that mosquitoes carry the West Nile virus, I am likely to be wrong most of the time when I judge individual mosquitoes to be carriers of the disease. But if I do get bitten by a mosquito carrying the virus, I may develop a serious illness. Although I am likely to be wrong a lot of the time, my error is worth it because I will take precautions against all mosquitoes, infected or not. This reduces my likelihood of contracting the disease.

Next, consider a stereotype about a social group: Scottish people drink too much. According to a press release summarising a 2025 report from Public Health Scotland, ‘people in Scotland are drinking 50 per cent above safe limits’. The stereotype may lead me to make accurate judgments in many cases but, when we consider the costs of the errors that I do make, my failure to treat those Scots as individuals and focus on them and their personal circumstances harms them. Indeed, this failure is sometimes claimed to constitute the intrinsic wrong of stereotyping. The costs of my errors need not be borne by me for me to take them into account. My generic beliefs about social categories may, therefore, need to meet a higher standard than those about, say, mosquitoes, since there is more at stake, morally speaking, when I make errors about other people.

The child who approaches the XL Bully expecting it to behave like their friendly golden retriever is making a dangerous mistake because they have overgeneralised from their experiences with their tame pet. The costs of that mistake might be very high. But what this example obscures is that many of the generalisations that the child makes on the basis of their experiences with their pet are true: dogs bark, dogs have four legs, dogs eat meat, dogs are furry. If the child failed to draw those conclusions from their admittedly meagre evidence, their knowledge of the world would be severely impoverished. What matters is that the child tests these generalisations against new evidence. And while it might be reckless, it is by approaching the XL Bully that they learn of their mistake. Popper would have approved.

Our need to generalise is in tension with the requirement that we respect each other’s autonomy. This is a tension between a cognitive obligation – to simplify experience and so make it comprehensible – and a moral one – to treat one another as individuals in all their rich specificity. It is easy to confuse a moral failing for a cognitive one but, when we criticise someone for overgeneralising or even stereotyping, we should remember how essential that cognitive shortcut is. Even stereotypes are part of the system with which we meet the future. To abandon that system wholesale would be to lose the in-built tools that enable us to focus on what is truly new.
