item.title: Sasquatch science
item.dc:creator: Andrew Bartlett & Jamie Lewis
item.description:
The hunt for Bigfoot sounds like the opposite of good science, but those pursuing the creature are often serious empiricists

- by Andrew Bartlett & Jamie Lewis

Read on Aeon
item.content:encoded:
Listen to this essay

23 minute listen

How do you go about capturing a monster? The search for Bigfoot, or Sasquatch – often referred to as Bigfooting – may sound like a whimsical endeavour: an activity of tall tales and cartoonish representations. Yet if you spend time listening to what Bigfooters themselves have to say, you discover a different picture.

We did exactly that. To research our book, Bigfooters and Scientific Inquiry: On the Borderlands of Legitimate Science (2026), we conducted more than 160 interviews, mostly with classical Bigfooters, who spend time in the forests of North America, collecting evidence and, as they see it, acting responsibly, rationally and scientifically.

As sociologists of science, we began with a simple premise: whatever one thinks about whether Bigfoot actually exists as a biological creature, Bigfooting undeniably does. If Bigfooting is a community – or set of communities – that are collecting, analysing, sharing, validating and contesting evidence, then Bigfooting is a suitable object of sociological enquiry. And so, we went on our own hunt to track down Bigfooters and make sense of how they themselves make sense of the world.

Before we began our sociological exploration of Bigfooting, we were cautioned that Bigfooters were anti-science. The truth is much more complex. Yes, Bigfooters work in opposition to mainstream institutional science, making claims about the world that do not accord with the scientific consensus. However, our research revealed that Bigfooters are not dismissive of scientific principles. In fact, many are dedicated empiricists who employ methodologies modelled on those found in professional scientific research. As George Eberhart, a cryptozoologist and Bigfooter, explained to us: ‘It’s not a part of mainstream science, it really isn’t. But you can apply a scientific method, or a journalistic method to it, to get some good science out of it.’

Yet Bigfooters are not ‘citizen scientists’ in the way we might be familiar with, due to their counter-establishment orientation and alternative vision of what ‘good’ science means. To a degree, the Bigfooter scientific model echoes that of the natural philosophers of previous centuries, in which individualism was valorised, and where testimony, anecdote and personal experience carried evidential weight.

So, how do contemporary Bigfooters use scientific technologies and techniques in their pursuit of evidence – and, ultimately, proof? And what makes their commitment to empiricism different from mainstream science?

Following our interviews, one particular line stuck with us as an apt description of the empirical Bigfooter’s mindset. It came from Cliff Barackman, the presenter of the US TV series Finding Bigfoot (2011-) and the owner of the North American Bigfoot Center in Boring, Oregon. ‘There is this foolish statement, that is still thrown around, that there is no evidence for Bigfoot,’ Barackman said. ‘There’s plenty of evidence, there’s no proof. There’s a big difference.’

Bigfooters have collected thousands of witness testimonies, cast hundreds of footprints, recorded scores of howls

This is what we might call the Bigfooter’s lament, and maybe the most concise summary of the frustration – and perhaps sadness – that Bigfooters experience when it comes to making empirical claims for Bigfoot’s existence.

Because there is ‘plenty of evidence’; Bigfooters have collected thousands of witness testimonies, cast hundreds of footprints, recorded scores of howls, and have even captured the occasional photograph or video. Of course, none of these are convincing if starting from the position that Bigfoot does not exist as a biological creature.

Bigfooters are thus faced with an evidential challenge that cannot be resolved with witness testimonies, photos, footprints or recorded sounds and groans. Implicitly and explicitly, both the general public and the scientific community make a simple request: Habeas corpus. Show the body.

‘On the side of science, they’re absolutely right. “Where’s the body? Where are the bones?” That’s what everybody asks, right?’ says Les Stroud, creator of the Canadian TV series Survivorman (2005-), which focused on Bigfoot for a season in 2015.

Over the decades, bodies have been presented, but these are almost unanimously considered to be hoaxes. For example, in the 1960s, the promoter Frank Hansen showcased a hairy humanoid figure encased in ice, initially supposedly found in Siberia and dubbed the Sibirskoye Creature, but more commonly known as the Minnesota Iceman. It had dubious provenance, but some took it seriously. Bernard Heuvelmans and Ivan T Sanderson, two of the founders of cryptozoology, examined the ‘body’, and wrote rival papers. In 1969, Heuvelmans published his description in Bulletin de L’Institut Royal des Sciences Naturelles de Belgique in which he claimed it was a new species, Homo pongoides, while Sanderson wrote up his findings in the US magazine Argosy and the Italian journal Genus, in which he claimed the body was that of Homo erectus. The primatologist John Napier, impressed by Heuvelmans’s description, attempted to get the Smithsonian Institution involved, and reports suggested that the FBI had an interest in the body. Napier, however, concluded that the Iceman was a fake, in line with the overwhelming consensus. Nevertheless, some Bigfooters maintain that the Iceman had been at some point a genuine body, and both Heuvelmans and Sanderson held to the belief that the body they had examined was only later replaced by a fake.

This continued absence of a body has led Bigfooters to weigh ethical dilemmas, outside the strict frameworks of university ethics committees. In particular, to kill, or not to kill? Bigfooters have fiercely discussed the question, with some advocating the merits of hunting Bigfoot, and others for a programme of foraging for traces. The anthropologist Grover Krantz, one of Bigfoot’s rare academic champions, supported efforts to find a specimen, up to and including the killing of a Bigfoot. One Bigfooter told us that Krantz even offered him money. ‘I won’t tell you how much, but a considerable amount of money to go work with him and try to collect a specimen in the Blue Mountains,’ said John Mionczynski, a notable outdoorsman who has been involved in mainstream conservation projects, and has been studying Bigfoot since the 1970s. They parted company over the issue. Others we interviewed were more bullish. Angelo Capparella, a member of the North American Wood Ape Conservancy (NAWAC), argued that killing a Bigfoot and bringing back the body is a scientific necessity. ‘Maybe it’s my bias as being trained as a museum scientist – one of my degrees – but a physical specimen is what it is going to take,’ Capparella told us. ‘We’re going to be spinning our wheels forever if we don’t get a specimen.’

However, most Bigfooters that we spoke to are, in principle, against killing a Bigfoot. Craig Woolheater, the co-founder of the Texas Bigfoot Research Centre, the precursor to NAWAC, told us that, since the Bigfoot population is unknown, killing one ‘may doom a family group, you know? [It] may doom their population.’

You may wonder, though, how do Bigfooters explain why no one has found a body whose owner died of natural causes? Not even a body part. Thousands of hikers and outdoorspeople have reported Bigfoot encounters, so why has not one of them found a corpse, a skeleton or even a bone? Some Bigfooters claim that this is naivety, based on ignorance of the natural world. The Bigfooter Russell Jones maintained that ‘hikers don’t find dead bears in the woods, and they’re not finding skeletons.’ These explanations may be unconvincing. Regardless of how infrequently hikers might stumble over a bear’s body, their corpses do exist; from private homes, to hotels, to museums, North America is replete with taxidermied examples.

Yet this absence itself can form the basis of a knowledge claim about Bigfoot. Among the explanations for the absence of a body or bones is the claim that Bigfoot is an intelligent, social creature. As the Bigfooter Todd Prescott told us: ‘I don’t know why that is [why we have not found a body], and I can guess, I can say what others have said: that they’re very careful and they’re never alone. So, when one dies, possibly they take that carcass away, they eat it, they bury it, and they bury it high and they bury it deep, so the chances of finding it on a mountaintop buried, you know, six feet under are remote at best.’

So, without bodies or bones, in recent years Bigfooters have sought smaller fragments of evidence – and it is here that empirical methods have blossomed.

The hope is that wrapped within the threads of Bigfoot hair is the veritable ‘blueprint’ of the creature itself

For starters, Bigfooters in the field routinely collect hair, which can now be brought back and examined, both under a microscope and by more sophisticated techniques. Bigfooters claim that Bigfoot hair has distinctive features compared with the hair of other animals, and only a skilled and knowledgeable observer can distinguish between them. A member of the Olympic Project, a Bigfoot research group, told us that ‘Sasquatch hair will be between 60 to 90 micrometres in width, flexible, [with] usually the same colour running the lengths of the hair. Under the microscope, the root has to be round or egg-shaped. The length of the hair usually will not have a core or medulla, it’ll be translucent, unless it’s really, really black, then it’s hard to see through the hair … but you look at the scale pattern on the hair. It has to be what we call imbricate scale pattern, just like a human.’

This is a detailed taxonomic description. For Bigfooters, the credibility of these knowledge claims is supported by a sliver of endorsement from institutional science. The late zoologist Wolf Henner Fahrenbach of Oregon Regional Primate Research Center is cited as the source of the claim that Bigfoot hair samples are those of a primate, but not those of any known primate.

For Bigfooters seeking such samples, the hope is that wrapped within the threads of Bigfoot hair is the veritable ‘blueprint’ of the creature itself: its genetic material. All other forms of evidence, witness statements, footprint casts, even microscopic examination of the hairs themselves, would be superseded by the certainty attached to genetics – and especially to the three letters, DNA – a science inextricably linked in the popular imagination to resolving questions of identity and identification.

Samples of hair, putatively that of a Bigfoot, have been analysed by the laboratories of institutional science, but the results have been inconclusive so far. Somewhat famously, the geneticist Bryan Sykes, then at the University of Oxford, conducted DNA testing on several examples of ‘Bigfoot’ hair for the UK TV series Bigfoot Files (2013). However, in a paper on the topic, he concluded that ‘the hairs were from a range of known extant mammals’.

Some Bigfooters argue that putative Bigfoot hair samples characteristically lack a central medulla, making it difficult to extract a DNA sample. Others reject the technique for other reasons. Alex Solunac, co-founder of the Vancouver Island Sasquatch Society, told us that, while ‘for years … I always had all my equipment ready for any kind of hair samples we’d come across,’ he came to realise ‘that, really, hair samples won’t do anything.’ Even if an unidentifiable sample were found and it ‘doesn’t match with anything else, it doesn’t mean that it’s Sasquatch, right?’

Yet hair is not the only possible source of Bigfoot genetic material. Shelly Covington-Montana, frustrated with the evidential value of witness accounts, resolved to do something to add scientific weight to Bigfooting. ‘When I showed up at the Olympic Project,’ she told us, ‘I decided “OK, if I’m going to bring gifts, why not wildlife DNA kits?”’ Covington-Montana looked into buying commercially available wildlife DNA kits, but ‘they were super expensive. That’s why I made my own, and I’ve gone through probably, I think, about six different upgrades, and now they’re up to human standards completely. I order in bulk from medical suppliers.’

In developing her own kits for Bigfooters in the field, Covington-Montana drew inspiration from empirical forms of knowledge-making outside institutional science, describing how she ‘talked to police officers and detectives, and anybody that I could get information from about how to go about it the best I could.’ In this, we can hear an echo of the way in which the Bigfoot Field Researchers Organization, the most prominent Bigfooting group, legitimises the use of witness testimonies by pointing out that they’re used in journalism and in law courts. Covington-Montana, however, makes a distinction, not only in that DNA is material evidence, but ‘it’s about spreading that idealism of the science, [and that] doing it through a citizen science aspect is way more interesting than making stuff up or promoting something you heard.’

Genetic evidence will allow Bigfooters to make definitive, material connections between Bigfoot encounters across North America

But if putative Bigfoot hair is not a good source of DNA, given that it characteristically lacks a central medulla, how might Bigfooters obtain genetic material? Covington-Montana works closely with Doug Hajicek – the producer of the US TV series MonsterQuest (2007-10) – who told us: ‘Oh, there’s some new types of evidence. One that I’ve identified is very important is skin sebum. Or just, you know, skin oil of possible Sasquatches. One, they seem to have a thicker, waxier-appearing, lighter skin oil. So, when they touch a surface – a car door, a window, a camper, an object, a cooler – they’re leaving these big handprints, including also face prints on houses, windows of cabins, and so on.’

Covington-Montana and Hajicek explained to us that, while in the past, Bigfooters had only used these oily impressions to attempt to draw finger- and handprints, they were now able to conduct chemical analyses – with Hajicek maintaining that ‘every great ape, including humans, has different amounts of things like triglycerides, cholesterol … So, we can get the latent details. We can get the chemical compounds of these prints.’

Now Bigfooters even hope to collect skin cells for DNA analysis. As Hajicek told us: ‘I’m in conversations every week with the top DNA labs all over the country. They feel they can pull a whole sequence if we can get up to 20 skin cells.’ Hajicek describes this as ‘much better than any photographic or video evidence. Or footprint evidence’ – as genetic evidence will allow Bigfooters to make definitive, material connections between encounters with Bigfoot across North America.

Underpinning these efforts is the democratisation of biotechnologies, which has put genetic analysis in the hands of people outside the boundaries of institutional science. Not only has there been a proliferation of contract research organisations of the kind discussed by Hajicek, but also a rise of direct-to-consumer genetic services. Of course, none are set up to analyse Bigfoot DNA. As Haskell Hart, technical consultant at the Bigfoot Enigma Research Center and Museum in Oklahoma, told us, this has led Bigfooters down molecular dead ends, since these labs deal only with human DNA. ‘No matter what sample [they] sent in there, it would only give human contamination,’ he said.

So, alongside cell analysis, Bigfooters have begun to look to other advances in institutional science, in this case ‘environmental DNA’ (eDNA) analysis, which is used in, for example, conservation projects. This could, in principle, allow putative Bigfoot habitats to be screened for the barest of molecular traces. Solunac notes that even the smallest threads of genetic evidence legitimise larger claims. ‘Maybe that DNA won’t match anything else,’ he said, ‘but we have DNA, we can look at the structure of it and see what it’s close to. Ah, it’s close to human, but it’s not; … it’s close to the orangutan but it’s not that either.’

The search for physical evidence of Bigfoot has been disappointing, tipping some into scepticism

While collecting and analysing eDNA requires expertise, it does not require individual Bigfooters to understand precise details. The Bigfooter Robert Leiterman describes eDNA analysis as being like ‘black magic right now’. As he tells it: ‘They go to a water source and anything that urinates in it, defecates in it, swims in it, slops off cells, is in the water, and they collect the sample and they come up with “Oh, these animals use this area”.’ It’s not black magic, of course, but black-boxed science – but here the Bigfooters can rely on the commercial bioscience sector to provide the necessary knowledge.

The feeling among Bigfooters appears to be that eDNA will not itself be ‘proof’ but will legitimise and extend existing claims, building what Hajicek described as ‘3D evidence’. For example, Barackman, the TV presenter, sees potential in linking genetic analysis with the study of putative nests and footprints found on the Olympic Peninsula in Washington state. ‘I think eDNA is going to be a huge key to unlocking this puzzle in the future,’ he said; ‘eDNA is going to be key in studying [Bigfoot] and learning about their behaviours over the long term.’

For many Bigfooters committed to a programme of naturalistic enquiry, the search for physical evidence of Bigfoot has been disappointing, sometimes to the point of disillusionment, tipping some into scepticism. But for others, all these recent advances in biotechnology have provided new capacities, new possibilities.

What makes analysing genetic material particularly appealing to Bigfooters is that it is not just a fragment of a body, but something that stands in for the body as a whole. It may not be the corpse, bones or hair of a hulking, hirsute creature, but chains of amino acids can represent the ‘blueprint’ of a whole organism. And genetics could, in principle, be used to position a species vis-à-vis other species. With a sample of Bigfoot DNA, we could know what-it-is-not and could also know what-it-is-nearly.

This is one of the lesser-known stories of the search for Bigfoot; a series of disappointments to which Bigfooters have responded by co-opting the power of institutional science, the capacities of which have expanded and, more importantly, have become routinised and commercialised.

One of the key aspects of material evidence is that it can be brought back from the field and subjected to sceptical enquiry, in ways that witness accounts resist. The search for material traces, aided by the miniaturisation and portability of new technologies, allows Bigfooters to collect evidence without an immediate, close encounter with the elusive creature. Bigfoot does not need to be hunted if traces can be gathered in its absence. A field that has long been dominated by hunters and outdoorsmen is today also inhabited by a form of ‘citizen scientist’, armed with a pipette rather than a rifle. However, unlike the typical citizen scientist, these ones are not motivated to support the institutions of mainstream science.

So, how exactly are Bigfooters engaged in scientific work? Bigfooting is clearly empirical; it centres on the collection and interpretation of evidence, and we hope readers of this essay, and of our book, appreciate how seriously Bigfooters take this dimension of their work, even in the face of derision. Yet empiricism alone does not constitute ‘science’. From a sociological perspective, science is a social practice – one that is embedded in institutions, structured by norms, and sustained through processes of consensus-building and the demarcation of intellectual territories. Contemporary science is characterised by social features such as peer review, formal training, credentialing, and competition for funding, all of which are absent from the social worlds of Bigfooting.

The contrast is instructive. Not everyone can become a primatologist, at least not without years of specialised education and institutional affiliation, whereas virtually anyone can become a Bigfooter. Indeed, you, the reader, could begin tomorrow, perhaps not by joining an expedition in the Pacific Northwest, but certainly by taking part in discussions that assess and contest claims about evidence. This openness is a significant source of Bigfooting’s appeal, but it also limits its capacity to accrue wider epistemic credibility and authority. Whereas established fields demarcate themselves and exclude others in order to maintain legitimacy, in a process once described by the sociologist Thomas Gieryn as ‘boundary work’, Bigfooting is a much looser form of sociality. Further, many Bigfooters are constitutionally hostile to such boundaries as, in their minds, it is by just such boundary work that Bigfoot has been rendered an unfit object of scientific enquiry. Given their commitment to empiricism, it is not irrational for them to regard the process that has been key to their own marginalisation as contrary to the doing of good science.

And yet, Bigfooting collects evidence and makes claims that could be relatively easily incorporated into mainstream, institutional science. This is not parapsychology; Bigfoot demands no new forces be theorised. This is not ghost-hunting; Bigfoot requires no new classes of entity. This is not UFOlogy; the existence of Bigfoot as a newly discovered ape would not challenge our understanding of our place in the Universe. The irony is that, should Bigfooters succeed, Bigfooting will be undone as an activity. As Joshua Blu Buhs wrote in Bigfoot: The Life and Times of a Legend (2009): ‘Science would still be science; anthropological theory would have a new wrinkle but remain mostly intact. Scientists would move in once America’s great ape was captured, and the amateurs would be out.’

A striking meditation on inequality via the bold sculptures that sit amongst skyscrapers in Paris’s business district

- by Aeon Video

Watch on Aeon
item.content:encoded: Located west of Paris, La Défense is often called the most beautiful business district in Europe. With nearly 70 monumental works of art erected alongside its skyscrapers, the busy, opulent neighbourhood doubles as an open-air museum. In The Great Arc, the French animator Camille Authouart takes the audience on ‘a poetic and social stroll’ around La Défense, with her beautifully textured pastel animations of the district ultimately evolving into a surreal meditation on class and shared space. Authouart draws a connection between La Défense’s public art and an unhoused man she observed sleeping under the film’s titular arch and resting against Alexander Calder’s steel sculpture Araignée Rouge, noticing how they had each become invisible to rush hour commuters. Blurring boundaries between documentary, narrative and poetic storytelling, Authouart’s immersive work forms a layered examination of urban life.

item.dc:creator: Sam Dresser
item.description:
C P Snow’s ‘Two Cultures’ lecture provoked a savage response from fellow critic F R Leavis. What was at the heart of it all?

- by Sam Dresser

Read on Aeon
item.content:encoded:
Listen to this essay

34 minute listen

When Charles Percy Snow rose to deliver the Rede Lecture at the University of Cambridge in 1959, he had good reason to be satisfied with himself. By sensible tenacity he had reached an upper station of English society, an unlikely terminus for one raised by a lower-middle-class family from a suburb of Leicester. He had grown up surrounded by artisans and labourers, a distant but kindly father, three beloved brothers, and a smothering mother. But by his 55th year, around the time he presented his Cambridge lecture, one could find Snow living in the only red-brick building on Eaton Terrace in one of London’s prestigious neighbourhoods, issuing calmly authoritative opinions on books and politics and science. He was, to his happiness, considered a serious man, with opinions worth hearing.

Of the many opinions he expounded at formidable length over his lifetime, only the phrase he introduced in his Cambridge lecture remains relevant: the ‘two cultures’. Within a few years, his term passed into common speech, and it is still quoted, a lifetime later, by people who have never read a word of Snow. But after more than half a century of overuse, it’s largely been wrung of its original meaning so that today the two cultures refer rather blandly to distinctions between the sciences and the humanities, calling attention to two apparently incommensurable ways of going about understanding the world.

But this is a thin, surface reading of what Snow actually said. His real opinion of the two cultures differed dramatically from what is now remembered. It incited a chorus of commentary; many praised his pithy articulation of how we enquire into the world. But it struck one man as so obtuse, so grossly symptomatic of the times, that it warranted a violent public response. That man was the Cambridge English scholar F R Leavis. Three years after Snow’s lecture, he delivered an improbably savage rebuttal in which he called Snow, among other things, a ‘preposterous and menacing absurdity’. This confrontation between Snow and Leavis – two dramatically different thinkers, representing traditions long in tension – gets at something more fundamental than the worn phrase that survived it: our deepest and conflicting temperaments towards life.

According to the English novelist Anthony Powell, C P Snow was affable, and rather humourless, the sort of man who gladly recognised a joke in conversation but wouldn’t be caught telling one himself. He could almost be compared to a computer, given his literal cast of mind and extraordinary capacity for work. With his large bald head, surfeit of chins and thick glasses that magnified big, bemused eyes, Snow’s visage was ripe material for caricaturists. Private Eye magazine even ran an unkind poll asking its readers if ‘C P Snurd’ was not the ugliest public figure of the day (Snow promptly sued for libel, and won; the results of the poll, alas, were never released).

But mockery is the price of fame, and a price well worth paying for the class-conscious and title-titillated Snow (his name had recently been ornamented with a knighthood by the young Queen). In 1959, he was most of the way through writing his semi-autobiographical cycle of novels, Strangers and Brothers. He had published seven of an eventual 11, tracking the life of his shadow, Lewis Eliot, who spent much of his time dealing with lengthy bureaucratic squabbles, sometimes in government, sometimes in university (Snow coined the term ‘corridors of power’). The eighth instalment of the series, called The Affair, was just finished when Snow gave his lecture. It contains in its closing an immortal line of literature, which captures better than anything else the tenor of Snow: ‘sensible men,’ a character grimly announces, ‘usually reach sensible conclusions.’

When he approached the lectern on 7 May 1959, Snow set out to make an eminently sensible point to the attendees of the Rede Lecture, crowded into the august Senate House at Cambridge. He titled his lecture ‘The Two Cultures and the Scientific Revolution’ (having discarded his original title, ‘The Rich and the Poor’). Despite the prestige of the event, Snow had little reason to expect much of a reaction to his lecture. More than two years earlier, he had published much the same thesis in New Statesman magazine without making a ripple. But now the idea had found its time, and Snow, to his own surprise, conjured a tempest that blew his name across the continents.

The content of the talk itself was explosive, even if delivered in a tone of invincible modesty

Snow told the crowd that, though he was no longer a practising scientist (he trained as a physicist in the 1930s), he still closely followed scientific developments. But his vocation, he noted with delighted self-curiosity, was that of a working and acclaimed novelist. (Sometimes over-acclaimed: George Steiner once said that Strangers and Brothers made Snow a peer of Proust.) Snow claimed that this uncommon duality of a life spent in science and in literature gave him a rare vantage on the ‘intellectual society’ of the West. He would, he explained, go from spending the day in the company of scientists to dining in the evening with their counterparts, whom he termed ‘literary intellectuals’, or simply ‘intellectuals’.

From Snow’s experience with these scientists and literary men – all men – he discerned a deep cultural cleft. The scientists read literature, but not seriously (Charles Dickens comes to them as someone ‘extraordinarily esoteric, tangled and dubiously rewarding’). Meanwhile, the intellectuals have a shy respect for science, but couldn’t tell you quite what the Second Law of Thermodynamics is – which Snow decides is the scientific equivalent of not having read a single work of Shakespeare. And the two cultures are drifting further apart:

Thirty years ago the cultures had long ceased to speak to each other: but at least they managed a kind of frozen smile across the gulf. Now the politeness has gone, and they just make faces.

This divergence disquiets Snow, and one would think from how his diagnosis is remembered that the purpose of the lecture was to call for a rapprochement between the cultures. In fact, Snow considered the lecture – and much of his work – to be an honest effort at mediation. But the content of the talk itself was explosive, even if delivered in a tone of invincible modesty. ‘The Two Cultures’ is incendiary, made more provocative by the pose he initially assumes as a disinterested diplomat ready to scurry between the two camps. He is, in fact, a highly motivated and partisan agent of the scientists.

Snow locates the origin of difference between the scientists and the intellectuals in their varying attitudes toward humankind’s existential situation. He intones that:

the individual condition of each of us is tragic. Each of us is alone: sometimes we escape from solitariness, through love or affection or perhaps creative moments, but those triumphs of life are pools of light we make for ourselves while the edge of the road is black: each of us dies alone.

Life is brief and brutal – and, confronted with this stark fact, how is one to respond? For Snow there are two options: supine submission to fate, or heroic struggle against the inevitable. ‘There is plenty in our condition which is not fate, and against which we are less than human unless we do struggle,’ he says. That is: one could be a scientist, striving to make the world a better place to live in, or one could be an intellectual, ‘complacent in one’s unique tragedy, and let the others go without a meal.’

Caring about bettering this life sets the two apart: the scientists do, and the intellectuals don’t. Snow’s argument then ratchets up rather abruptly when he intimates that the literary folks should be blamed, in part, for Auschwitz, though fortunately this isn’t a line of thought he follows. What he does say, however, is that the complacency of intellectuals makes them yearn for a yesterday that never was and yet also wish ‘the future did not exist’. In support of this, Snow looks to the Industrial Revolution, which ‘the traditional culture didn’t notice: or when it did notice, didn’t like what it saw.’ Intellectuals may be content contemplating an invented past, when things were supposedly seamless and simple, but in the face of modernity and its challenges, they ‘shuddered away’; their novels and poems ‘not in effect more than screams of horror’. It’s clear to Snow that the Industrial Revolution was a Good Thing, since he says that ‘Industrialisation is the only hope of the poor.’ So what would that make the intellectuals? ‘Natural Luddites’ were his exact words.

Snow considered scientific research to be in and of itself a moral act

Snow was nothing if not a practical man, and he declares that, on practical terms, political power must be wrested from the traditionalists, otherwise Britain will sunset before its time, like the decadent Doges of the long-lost Venetian Republic (then a common image of decline). Snow goes on to elaborate his view on education, and to some muddled extent the Cold War, but by now the sensible point has been made: that society must turn away from the ‘feline and oblique’ intellectuals and towards the scientists, who, you’ll be relieved to know, are ‘steadily heterosexual’ (as he described them in the New Statesman).

He sees these scientists as strong men, willing to wrestle with the tragedy of existence by increasing the amount of happiness in the world. That struggle makes them optimists. They ‘have the future in their bones’, Snow declaims, and it is this that also makes them more moral than the intellectuals (he considered scientific research to be in and of itself a moral act). Their minds, honed by contact with the real, innocent facts of the world, can grapple with its ailments, namely poverty and the Cold War. Being conversant in the ways and discoveries of scientists, then, is the best way to be fully modern, fully of our time. Science is the morally necessary stance to take towards the world in order to truly understand it and make it better. And just how do the scientists do this? Technology, mostly, which can be used to alleviate life’s brutality for the impoverished ‘common men’ throughout the world. Material comfort is the ultimate aim.

Toward the end of the lecture, Snow counsels that the country needs a substantial investment in the education of scientists, who with technocratic coolness will one day hold the reins of power and steer Albion towards a happy future. Science is the solution, and because of its quantitative rigour, able scientists can quickly be identified and elevated – the perfect meritocratic system, which hugely appealed to Snow, who made his way to the top not by land or by family but by good, hard, sensible work.

Public reaction to Snow’s lecture was swift and divisive. The Spectator magazine printed letters about the two cultures for months, and many important people in Britain, and eventually the United States, debated it. Senator John F Kennedy called it ‘one of the most provocative discussions that I have ever read of the intellectual dilemma.’

Snow, for his part, was winningly humble about the hubbub: a few years later, he said that it ‘was clear that many people had been thinking on this assembly of topics. The ideas were in the air.’ Which is true. If anything – and that’s a singular if – the originality of the lecture lies in its unabashed endorsement of science over the humanities, not in any fine distinctions or diagnoses. Indeed, the tone of Snow’s lecture approached the indignant clarity of a manifesto. In the aftermath, his reputation reached its apotheosis. The prime minister Harold Wilson briefly appointed him to the Ministry of Technology, and Snow ascended once again to become a baron in 1964. He chose as his motto Aut Inveniam Viam aut Faciam: I will either find a way or make one. Lord Snow expected the Nobel Prize in due course.

But by the time of his barony, Snow’s name had become linked to someone who had a rather different view of the issues confronting modernity. In fact, this man seemed to hate him with thoroughgoing ferocity. So comprehensive was it that Snow later blamed him for the stubborn lack of a Nobel. If it was any recompense to Snow – and it wasn’t – the literary critic Frank Raymond Leavis was an insufferable prick to pretty much everyone.

In February 1962, almost three years after Snow gave his diagnosis of science and literature, Leavis delivered the Richmond Lecture at Downing College, Cambridge, ominously titled ‘The Two Cultures? The Significance of C P Snow’. Leavis was small, angular, large-collared, with a potent gaze that unnerved his students. He ‘was Seriousness personified’, recalled Clive James. ‘He even had a serious way of being bald.’ In the early 1960s, Leavis was at the height of influence, and the twilight of his teaching career.

The Evening Standard predicted ‘Stormy Don’s Swan Song Should Be A Fiery One’

For a generation, Leavis had exercised his will on English Literature at Cambridge, shaping the sensibilities of readers over decades. Indeed, he did more than anyone else, save I A Richards, to turn literature into a fit subject of rigorous academic enquiry. He was zealous, loved, loathed and extraordinarily successful. Noel Annan called him a ‘deviant’ of the age, a ‘don who despised scholarship as pedantry, a critic who called for collaborative enterprise yet considered compromise as treachery, a moralist who demanded writers – in fact everybody – should be judged by a single standard.’ Nevertheless, five years after Leavis’s death in 1978, Terry Eagleton could still write that there ‘is no more need to be a card-carrying Leavisite today than there is to be a card-carrying Copernican.’

Given his stature, the press took an interest when Leavis announced he had something to say about Snow’s thesis. The BBC even wanted to record the lecture, but Leavis refused. Several reporters were present, however, and the hall was packed and full of expectation, fanned by an article in the Evening Standard that predicted ‘Stormy Don’s Swan Song Should Be A Fiery One’.

It was. Leavis promptly informed his audience that Snow ‘is as intellectually undistinguished as it is possible to be’, an ‘intellectual nullity’, and ‘portentously ignorant’. While outraged Cantabrigians angrily quit the hall, Leavis barrelled on imperviously: ‘Snow is, of course, a – no, I can’t say that; he isn’t; Snow thinks of himself as a novelist.’ It was not just that he was a deficient writer, ‘for as a novelist he doesn’t exist; he doesn’t begin to exist. He can’t be said to know what a novel is.’ On and on, Leavis torched his target. Snow’s lecture was distinguished by ‘a show of knowledgeableness’ that Leavis claimed he wouldn’t permit in a group discussion, ‘let alone a pupil’s essay’. Snow’s ‘unconsciousness is an essential characteristic’; ‘a mind to be argued with – that is not there.’ Then the speaker paused to assure his audience, quite unconvincingly: ‘Don’t, I beg, suppose that I am enjoying a slaughterous field-day.’

Leavis’s invective yanked the focus of the debate from the nature of intellectual life in postwar Britain to an examination into precisely how stupid the roundheaded nonentity from Leicester really was. Pretty much everybody, on both sides of the Atlantic, was appalled by Leavis’s cruelty, by the searing petulance so unexpectedly served up in the hallowed halls of an ancient university. The English writer Hilary Corke, after allowing that Snow’s lecture was ‘not very original’, spoke for many startled onlookers when he wrote that ‘there is really not the slightest reason why the thought of the good Snow should bring blood-flecked froth to the mouth.’

But froth Leavis did. Why? Because, for Leavis, Snow had become a symbol of the times, the primary example of its vacuity, its thoughtlessness, its bloodlessness. The point is that for Snow to be considered a ‘sage’ – and he was – then something very wrong had happened to intellectual life. As Leavis says, it was the fact that prospective students of Downing College, Cambridge continued to reference Snow’s lecture in their applications that set him off – as if Snow was anything like the ‘great English novelists’ that he once enumerated with typical definitiveness (Jane Austen, George Eliot, Henry James and Joseph Conrad). In a world attuned to the values of great literature, Snow would’ve been laughed into annihilation; instead, he was crowned a leader of thought. So, in taking down Snow, Leavis meant to take down the whole soulless system that had raised him up in the first place.

The infelicitous name that Leavis chose for this system was ‘technologico-Benthamism’. Leavis did not mean by this classification anything political. In fact, his politics overlapped with Snow’s. As Guy Ortolano writes in his excellent book The Two Cultures Controversy (2009), they ‘shared a commitment to meritocratic ideals, along with a corresponding hostility towards egalitarian demands – both of which they expressed by defending elites.’ They were snobby liberals who disdained Marxists as much as fascists, if not more, and proud Englishmen who were unthinking defenders of their ‘natural’ rights and privileges. ‘If ever two men were committed to England, Home, and Duty,’ wrote the American critic Lionel Trilling in 1962, ‘they are Leavis and Snow.’ But Leavis was ultimately invested in ideas and literature as he understood them, not the grime of the day-to-day, and it’s notable that the virulent interwar debates on pacifism, rearmament, communism and the General Strike seemed not to interest him very much (though the quarterly review he founded, Scrutiny, had its political dimensions and would influence the next generation of highly engaged critics such as Raymond Williams, Richard Hoggart and Stuart Hall). Naturally, the future Minister of Technology was more responsive to events, but his political predictions, especially at the opening of the Second World War, are striking for how consistently and assertively wrong they were.

Then what did Leavis mean by ‘technologico-Benthamism’? What is this heartless system that anointed Snow and invited such ruthless contempt? It is the stance one takes towards the world that makes analytical and reductive thinking the most promising path towards truth and wellbeing. It is shaped by the idea of utility, and it speaks the evidently precise language of logic and formulae. It aims for rigour, for certitude – for the cool satisfaction of correct answers to solvable problems. It is systematic, conceptual, and feeds off data rather than anecdote; objectivity is valued more than subjectivity. It is materialistic and tends to assume that language is a reasonably accurate reflection of reality. It is gratifyingly commonsensical. Right words rightly put would give one a sense of how the world is, in and of itself – that is to say, simplistically, that ‘science’ is ‘true’. To understand the world, one must be conversant in science and its morphing conclusions, responsive to its methods, deferential to its practitioners. It is this style of thought, or approach to life, that Leavis sees as having launched Snow to his unearned heights – all while draining British culture of any meaningful vitality.

It was just this drab preoccupation with exactness that bothered Leavis

With the intensity of a paranoiac, Leavis saw technologico-Benthamism everywhere he looked: the Sunday papers, the Wilson government, the recent statistical turn in the social sciences. And it’s not difficult to find exemplars of technologico-Benthamism in British history. Jeremy Bentham, of course, and his utilitarian epigones arrayed against Coleridge and his romantic mystifications; optimistic men of science like Thomas Huxley and H G Wells taking on the more aesthetically inclined likes of Matthew Arnold and Walter Pater; and J B S Haldane, a friend of Snow’s, who in his debate with Bertrand Russell in the 1920s foresaw unbelievable technological progress tempered by ethical stasis. John Stuart Mill glossed the distinction with acuity: ‘By Bentham … men have been led to ask themselves … Is it true? And by Coleridge, What is the meaning of it?’ In the 20th century, when scientists became more influential, and technological advancement bemused and inspired the public, Leavis saw the cold quantitativeness of technologico-Benthamism stultifying culture to a tragic degree.

Above all, this style of thought valued analysis and exactness, and it was just this drab preoccupation with exactness that bothered Leavis, for it neglected what he considered should be the true focus of serious thinking: ‘life’. The idea of life haunts Leavis’s thought. It is central to it and yet maddeningly opaque. He believed the mark of great literature – or rather, what it is that makes great literature great – is its ability to manifest life, to summon it and make it exist for the attentive and dedicated reader. Literature is the locus of life. If a piece of writing does not make the close reader somehow sense life, then it can fairly be denied the status of literature. The absence of life is the most common cause of Leavis’s derision, with which he was so generous (even extending once to a rant against Jimi Hendrix, of all people). So: what did he mean by it? What is life?

Unfortunately, to have even asked this is, for Leavis, already to have misunderstood life. Life cannot be adequately defined. It is too big for that – too fluid, too profound, too inexhaustible, too limitless. The few times Leavis actually stooped to give some modicum of an indication about what this word is doing in his thinking, he barely did more than gesture. ‘Life (which is creativity),’ he once wrote parenthetically. Ortolano attempted to sum up Leavis’s definition of life as ‘the creative act at the core of what it meant to be human’. Near his death, Leavis said: ‘Life is growth and change in response to changing conditions.’ But none of these are robust definitions: he’s hardly saying more than ‘life is alive’.

As Eagleton later scorned: ‘If you asked for some reasoned theoretical statement of [the definition of life], you had thereby demonstrated that you were in the outer darkness: either you felt Life or you did not.’ Aldous Huxley, in his novel Point Counter Point (1928), had made a similarly sardonic remark:

Burlap’s belief in Life was one of the things Walter found most disturbing. What did the words mean? Even now he hadn’t the faintest idea. Burlap had never explained. You had to understand intuitively; if you didn’t you were as good as damned. Walter supposed that he was among the damned.

Many have been content to count among the damned. There’s no doubt that such a view of life was wilfully exclusionary, not dissimilar from the keepers of ancient esoteric truths. Indeed, Leavis was an out-and-out elitist whose overarching purpose at Downing College was to create a caste of literary hierophants who would possess a rarified understanding of life, preserve the highest of high culture, and duly dispense correct opinions to the befuddled masses. That whole endeavour can strike us today as rather silly or perhaps even authoritarian. But shorn of his cult-building, Leavis’s attitude towards life deserves to be taken seriously because it is not, historically, an unusual view.

For Leavis, Snow represents the denial of life, the disregard for its mystery

The urge to gesture towards things that do not seem possible to articulate is common, perhaps ubiquitous. The limits of language – that is, what is permissible to say about the world so that others may understand you and disagree with you – are by nature fluid. Our experience of being is neither fully captured by our awareness nor by our language. To adapt the American philosopher Richard Rorty, a part of our dealings with the world, especially when we’re thinking philosophically, is the effort to say what hasn’t been said before, to try to put into words sensations or phenomena that haven’t yet been. It’s what people do in these moments, when confronted in an immediate way with the feeling of trying to say the unsayable, or encountering things that in some sense seem too expansive for the confines of words, that tends to demarcate certain approaches to how one lives. For some, logic, exactitude, quantification, definition and analysis hold out the promise of greater understanding about ourselves and the world. For Leavis, in sensing life in great literature, it was necessary to leave its mystery unblemished by attempts at analysis, or quantification, or definition. That is, life’s essential mystery is best illuminated by not making it explicit, but by showing, through works of great literature, where life could be found.

For Leavis, ‘life’ is not something ‘out there’ to be sought or communed with. It’s not like a spirit or a God. It’s rather a secular disposition that searches for the extraordinary qualities of the present, the quotidian. It imbues the natural with the supernatural – a hallmark of Romantic thought according to the American critic M H Abrams, and one that also marks Leavis’s thought. And it is a profoundly personal experience to sense the life that courses through great literature.

Leavis’s approach to literary criticism stresses the personal encounter, as when he fairly summed up how to deal with art, with life, in his Richmond Lecture. To the question ‘This is so, isn’t it?’, an interlocutor replies: ‘Yes, but – .’ As the critic Chris Joyce explained, the ‘but’ stands ‘for reservations, qualifications, and so on.’ It is not that each encounter with literature produces incommensurable and utterly idiosyncratic responses so that, in those vapid words, ‘everyone is right’. It is that, by navigating literature with others by way of ‘Yes, but …’, better judgments will be alighted upon.

Leavis says that technologico-Benthamism, defined by its scientism and its devotion to logic and clarity, cannot account for everything that can be thought. To him and others with a sympathy for inexhaustibility and ineffability, the promoters of technologico-Benthamism seem to hold that they can either ignore or explain away the mystery of life, or that it can somehow be tamed and stilled by analysis. In this way, they are, to borrow from John Keats, not burdened by that mystery. That is what makes them so suspicious and what makes Snow – ‘the blind enlightened menace’ – so portentous. He represents the denial of life, the disregard for its mystery. By deflating the unnameable quality of life to such a dreary term as ‘standard of living’ – which is what Snow did – he threatens to ossify all that makes living interesting and creative. Snow and the technologico-Benthamites’ indefatigable certainty ignores something crucial to being human, and by ignoring it diminishes it.

Snow is like the minister of commerce in E T A Hoffmann’s anecdote, who, after listening carefully to a long symphony, asks the man sitting next to him: ‘And what, dear Sir, does that prove to us?’

The Spectator printed Leavis’s lecture a few weeks after he delivered it, and, wickedly, illustrated the issue with several insulting caricatures of Snow’s unusual face. Snow reported to a friend that he was ‘nettled’ by Leavis, though this is an understatement. In fact, he lurched into action by swiftly deploying his network of dignitaries to attack Leavis through letters, editorials and lectures. It was a coordinated if not very successful campaign, executed by his devoted friend the historian J H Plumb. Then Snow himself responded in the essay ‘The Two Cultures: A Second Look’ (1963). He didn’t mention Leavis by name, reiterated and (unnecessarily) stressed how simple his original thesis had been, and quibbled about how he had been misquoted. He speculated, too, about the emergence of a ‘third culture’ that would somehow bridge the gap between the original two (a project unconvincingly taken up by the American impresario John Brockman in the 1990s). It was not an effective outing.

Leavis, for his part, remained enchanted by himself. He sent his fulsome self-congratulations to friends and devotees. A ‘classic’, he deemed his lecture, and marvelled at its complete ‘unanswerableness’. But these loving reviews rather miss the mark: reading Leavis’s lecture today, one is still struck most of all by its vituperation, its overwhelming hatred for Snow and what he represents. Even without the abuse, much of what Leavis presumes – especially his idea of ‘life’ and literature – goes unsaid, and what Stefan Collini observed of Leavis’s criticism as a whole applies to the lecture: ‘one can encounter the disconcerting sense that the real work of analysis had always already been performed.’ That which had already been performed was the development of the mystical – some, including Leavis, say ‘religious’ – idea of life. It had been performed not only by Leavis, but by the long line of Romantic and mystical thinkers who preceded him.

Snow’s view of life, on the other hand, is not religious. It is not mysterious. It is solid and examinable and fashionably dull. When Snow says that the scientists want to improve people’s lives, he means that he wants people to have their material necessities taken care of so that they may do whatever they will, even if it’s embarking on a monstrous career in English at Downing College. But for Leavis, this idea that life can be whittled down to material comforts is entirely to miss the point of living in the first place, which he takes Snow himself to be so colourfully exhibiting.

It’s not necessary to try to resolve the two cultures, or to collapse them into one, or to invent a third

So, what of the two cultures today? The condition that Snow described more or less remains: there is indeed an obdurate incomprehensibility between the sciences and the humanities. From the vantage of the scientists, the humanities – some subjects more than others – are of dubious value if not purpose, an accusation that sometimes stings given the relentless and defensive soul-searching among humanities scholars (though this is also part of what it means to be engaged with the humanities at all). From their side, the incomprehensibility is both of the achievements of science itself, but also that the scientists think they can do without the humanities, as if their discipline can exist in a culture-less vacuum without scrutiny of non-scientific issues like morality, value, history and purpose. Of course, neither view is very fair.

But this is a surface-level understanding of the gap between the two cultures today. Snow and Leavis’s confrontation gets at something more fundamental. Their mutual incomprehensibility is better understood through the lens of a number of distinctions or dichotomies: technologico-Benthamism and life; science and literature; Snow and Leavis. These distinctions extract cross-sections of the two cultures at varying angles, suggesting tendencies, temperaments and emphases of each side. More dichotomies come to mind: utilitarianism and romanticism; tough-minded and tender-minded; Bentham and Coleridge; mechanical and dynamic; fact and interpretation; objective and subjective; thought and feeling; future and past; truth and meaning. There are no doubt many more.

When arrayed before us in such a way, it’s tempting to see in these dichotomies two poles of a conversation that extends back at least as far as Plato, and to see Snow’s two cultures as a sort of piquant formalisation of both. What William James said in 1907 about the history of philosophy can be applied to the two cultures: it is ‘to a great extent’ a ‘clash of human temperaments’. As such, it’s not necessary to try to resolve the two cultures, or to collapse them into one, or to invent a third. What we should consider instead is something simpler: what are we doing when we raise the question of the two cultures in the first place?

We are reflecting upon our intellectual and existential life in the widest possible arena. We are making judgments about varying ways of dealing with human experience. Of course these different approaches will clash, sometimes fruitfully, sometimes not. But raising the question of the two cultures is also to see the multiplicity of intentions people bring to their existence, the great varieties of hope people have for their labours and investigations; it is to engage in the irrepressible dialogue about what experience is about at the highest level because it asks questions of an ultimate nature. And this is what Leavis thought was the essence of literature, of art: to ask ‘What for – what ultimately for?’

item.title: The last ice age
item.dc:creator: Aeon Video
item.description:
Retracing his grandparents’ journey to Iceland’s Vatnajökull glacier, a writer draws on storytelling to grasp climate change

- by Aeon Video

Watch on Aeon
item.content:encoded:
The Icelandic writer and environmental activist Andri Snær Magnason traces both his love of storytelling and his concern for the natural world back to his grandparents. Amateur explorers, they volunteered on scientific expeditions to the Vatnajökull ice cap, even setting off the day after their wedding in 1956. Their stories, and the footage filmed by Magnason’s grandfather, shaped Magnason’s imagination and, later, his sense of urgency about climate change.

In this film by Emergence Magazine, the California-based filmmakers Adam Loften and Emmanuel Vaughan-Lee follow Magnason as he returns to Vatnajökull with his son, retracing his grandparents’ journey. Weaving together the family’s archival footage with present-day images of Magnason and his son at the ice cap, the film makes stark the dramatic changes that have taken place over the past seven decades. Throughout, the film shows how stories move us in a way that abstract ideas and data cannot: by connecting environmental loss to the people we hold close – past, present and future – they humanise our concern for the planet and raise the stakes of what we stand to lose.

item.title: Towards an AI for Africa
item.dc:creator: Fainos Mangena
item.description:
Western-developed AI rides roughshod over Ubuntu values of connection and community that animate African ethical life

- by Fainos Mangena

Read on Aeon
item.content:encoded:
Listen to this essay

17 minute listen

Imagine someone in Harare, Zimbabwe, turning to a large language model (LLM) for life advice, as many increasingly do: ‘I’ve been offered a promotion with a significant raise,’ she writes. ‘But it requires me to move far away from my community. What should I do?’ The answer she receives will depend, to some extent, on a certain set of values that informs how the LLM functions. And since artificial intelligence is a Western invention, these values often reflect their creators’ values – clashing with the culture of the person with the query. In the long run, her behaviour may be shaped by an LLM’s values, which she doesn’t intentionally share.

The difficulties of using AI in Africa are also linguistic. By the summer of 2025, only 42 languages in Africa were supported by an LLM, out of more than 2,000 found in the continent; 98 per cent of African languages have no meaningful AI support at all. If you don’t speak one of the languages supported by an LLM, which includes many millions of Africans, then you are denied the opportunities of AI. Just as Africa was excluded from the benefits of past industrial revolutions, so too is it being locked out of the AI revolution.

Linguistic and cultural exclusion shape Africa’s relationship with AI. There is nothing ethically neutral or objective about AI. Despite the designers’ pretensions toward universality, AI’s ethical framework reflects Western assumptions and biases. Deeply embedded in the technology itself are the values of its creators. The growth of AI therefore means the imposition of Western values – very much at the expense of Indigenous frameworks. This is ‘algorithmic colonialism’, in the words of the Ethiopian-born cognitive scientist Abeba Birhane: a new kind of colonialism every bit as destructive as the old.

In order to grasp the seriousness of this new colonialism, we should compare the Western values that undergird AI today with the Hunhu/Ubuntu ethical framework. ‘Hunhu/Ubuntu’ is the name given to the dominant moral tradition of sub-Saharan Africa, expressed in the Nguni/Shona proverb Umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu – a person is a person through other persons. Known as Hunhu in Shona-speaking communities of Zimbabwe and Zambia, and as Ubuntu in the Nguni languages of southern Africa, the tradition extends across a vast swathe of the African continent.

As Africans increasingly take up the use of AI, there is a real risk that their foundational ethical framework will be diminished or obscured by the subtle imposition through AI of Western values. So we must ask, to what extent are the principles of Hunhu/Ubuntu in conflict with Western values? And how might AI be developed inclusively so that it serves everyone, not just its creators?

The ideal of ‘responsible AI’ was aptly articulated by the philosopher and computer scientist Damian Okaibedi Eke and colleagues: it is ‘the idea of developing AI systems that will not only be compliant to laws (including human rights provisions) but that are socially/culturally sensitive and acceptable as well as ethically responsible.’ This is a high bar, and AI doesn’t come close to clearing it.

The major frameworks for ethical AI – guidelines issued by the European Commission’s High-Level Expert Group on AI, by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development, and by UNESCO – share a common vocabulary of fairness, transparency, accountability and human dignity. But the values founding these ideals derive from the Enlightenment liberalism of John Locke, Immanuel Kant and John Stuart Mill. Presented as universal, they are in reality particular, contingent and historically determined. And their particularity has formidable consequences because, when these frameworks are adopted globally, they do not appear as one ethical tradition among many, but as the universal standard – a kind of imperialism dressed up as common sense.

The baggage of neo-colonialism is found in the essential architecture of AI

Part of the problem is that these guidelines have not received enough input from African scholars and thinkers. A 2023 survey found that, of the then-existing 200 sets of AI ethics guidelines identified internationally, the vast majority originated in the Global North: North America, Europe and East Asia. Africa, home to around a billion people, contributed just a handful. This means that the ethical architecture being built into AI systems has been constructed almost entirely without reference to the moral traditions of a continent. The result is a technology that contradicts African values.

So what are the Western values embedded in AI? They can be boiled down to three: rationality, individualism and, most importantly, autonomy. The Western tradition places the individual at the centre of moral life. This is true across its major ethical theories. For Kant, every person is a sovereign lawgiver, an end in themselves. For the utilitarians, what matters is the aggregate of individual satisfactions; happiness is the only metric that matters. Even virtue ethics, the oldest of the three traditions dating back to Plato, locates moral excellence in the cultivation of the individual soul. They all share an assumption that the basic unit of ethics is the person, solitary and unencumbered. AI’s emphasis on individualism over communalism stems from this historical background.

Autonomy is the most vivid expression of this kind of individualism. As the South African philosopher Mogobe Ramose has argued, the Enlightenment principle of autonomy was bound up with a specific claim about who counted as fully rational – that is, white European men – and therefore who had the standing to govern themselves and others. This idea of autonomy is now coming to the Global South as part of the baggage of neo-colonialism, found in the essential architecture of AI: in the personalisation engines that treat each user as a sovereign individual with preferences to be satisfied, in the decision-making algorithms that optimise for individual outcomes, and in the governance frameworks that emphasise individual rights and individual accountability.

But Hunhu/Ubuntu ethics do not mesh well with these commitments, and the clash between these two value systems runs deeper than cultural emphasis. It goes to the most fundamental and searching question of what a person actually is, in the final analysis.

What is Hunhu/Ubuntu? Much of this framework can best be understood through proverbs, the most important of which is the aforementioned Umuntu ngubuntu ngabantu: a person is a person through other persons. The Kenyan philosopher John S Mbiti gave it its classic formulation: ‘I am because we are; since we are, therefore I am.’ This is a statement about the basic structure of human existence that is in serious tension with the Western view of individualised and atomised humans. The Hunhu/Ubuntu claim is that personhood is not something you are born with, but more like something you become, through dealings with other people. As the Nigerian-born philosopher Michael Onyebuchi Eze puts it, ‘a person’s humanity is dependent on the appreciation, preservation and affirmation of other person’s humanity.’

Hunhu/Ubuntu is a product of what I have termed the common moral position, which is built on four pillars: the group, dialogue, experience, and spirituality. The group is primary. Rume rimwe harikombi churu, as the Shona say: one man cannot surround an anthill. Moral knowledge is not acquired through individual reason working alone, a solitary discovery of what is good and bad, but through ongoing, evolving dialogue, above all at the dare, the communal court where elders mediate between the living and the ancestral world. Hunhu/Ubuntu ethics are also anchored in spirituality, meaning that the source of the African value system is the spirit world. Elders discover this ethical knowledge through experience, and they pass it on to the next generations. The Nigerian proverb is apt: what a father sees seated, the son cannot see standing.

The values that flow from these foundations are demanding. Community loyalty: everything you do should benefit the group you belong to; Hunhu/Ubuntu discourages self-seeking tendencies. Consensus-building: no single view carries the day until the collective has spoken. Of great importance when examining the differences between Hunhu/Ubuntu ethics and Western ethics is the issue of human dignity. In one of his most influential contributions, the American-born philosopher Thaddeus Metz argues that a human being has dignity insofar as she has the capacity for community, where community is characterised in terms of solidarity. An African cannot be said to have dignity if he or she does not contribute to the betterment of his or her group or community: ‘I am because we are; since we are, therefore I am.’ Shared responsibility, another important value, means that people and groups come together to find a solution to a common problem affecting their lives. Within the context of Hunhu/Ubuntu, challenges are not left to one individual to solve. Vanhu (the people) work together.

The clash between AI and Hunhu/Ubuntu is built into the logic of how AI systems work. AI is configured for the individual: its recommendation engines, personalisation algorithms and user interfaces treat each person as a sovereign agent, in much the same way that Kant and others regarded the inviolable person. The community, in AI’s architecture, is really an aggregate of individuals or a collection of data points, not its own living and organic entity to which those individuals belong and owe obligations. Hunhu/Ubuntu inverts this. As the Ghanaian theologian John S Pobee put it in Toward an African Theology (1979): Cognatus ergo sum – I belong, therefore I exist. Where AI begins with the individual and asks what she wants, Hunhu/Ubuntu begins with the community and asks what it needs.

This leads to several specific – and illuminating – conflicts between these two systems. The first is over agency. Hunhu/Ubuntu holds that meaningful human agency is collective, that the dare (communal court) is not a constraint on individual freedom but its greatest expression. AI substitutes machine agency for human collective agency: it makes decisions, ranks options, filters information and personalises outputs in ways that bypass deliberative community processes entirely.

AI nudges users to look out for themselves; Hunhu/Ubuntu tends toward looking out for each other

A second conflict is about the sacred. Hunhu/Ubuntu situates human life within a cosmological order in which God (Musikavanhu/Unkulunkulu/Nkosi) is the ultimate source of creative power, and human beings are stewards within that order rather than masters of it. AI’s ambitions are, meanwhile, unbounded: its most prominent proselytisers have proclaimed that the goal is to build machines that surpass human intelligence across all domains; to replicate the very capacities that the Hunhu/Ubuntu tradition holds to be divine. AI’s aspirations are rank hubris.

These tensions are visible in the way people actually use AI, and in the ways AI shapes behaviour over time. For instance, AI platforms optimise for individual economic advantage: personalised pricing, competitive job-matching algorithms, financial tools designed to maximise individual returns. Hunhu/Ubuntu’s economic intuition is the opposite. As researchers examining Ubuntu-based approaches to data governance have noted, the philosophy favours sharing over competition and equitable distribution over individual accumulation, what one study termed an ‘anticapitalist logic’ rooted in the principle that wealth has meaning only insofar as it benefits the community. AI meanwhile nudges users to look out for themselves; Hunhu/Ubuntu tends toward looking out for each other.

Or take decision-making. AI systems increasingly make or pre-structure consequential decisions about creditworthiness, medical triage and job applications on behalf of individuals, cutting out the communal deliberation that Hunhu/Ubuntu regards as morally essential. When an algorithm decides who gets a loan, there is no dare.

A third domain is privacy. Western AI ethics frames privacy as an individual right: your data belongs to you. But in many African contexts, information is not individual property but flows through households, clans and communities; decisions about data-sharing are properly made collectively, not by lone individuals. The entire architecture of digital consent assumes a model of personhood that goes against Hunhu/Ubuntu values.

The question, then, is: can Hunhu/Ubuntu principles be infused into AI to make it more inclusive? AI developers must prioritise Indigenous peoples and values. For example, the Geneva-based AI expert Jovan Kurbalija has argued that ‘when AI platforms provide advice to African citizens on family issues, health problems, and searching for jobs, to name a few, they have to reflect the local ethical and cultural milieu.’ This is the bare minimum that responsible AI requires. However, the reality on the ground is different. In 2025, African Business magazine noted that the vast majority of global training data reflects the experiences and priorities of high-income countries. This imbalance underscores the importance of developing local datasets and content that reflect African contexts.

A Hunhu/Ubuntu-informed AI would prioritise collective agency over individual preference, serve the common good rather than aggregate personal satisfactions, and build in transparency and accountability to the communities affected. And it would take environmental sustainability as an expression of Hunhu/Ubuntu’s commitment to the symbiotic relationship between humanity and nature, and to the intergenerational obligations that bind together the past and the future.

Translating Hunhu/Ubuntu values into the rules that AI governance requires is exquisitely hard work

There are, however, fundamental structural problems to accomplishing this. Africa has been excluded from the benefits of past industrial revolutions, just as it is from the current one, and according to the same logic: the Global North designs and exports the technology, forcing the Global South to accept it without any say in its standards or applications – a merely updated version of the old colonial harm.

And it’s worth wondering whether AI developers would cede ground in the first place by adopting a Hunhu/Ubuntu ethical framework. What’s in it for them? There is also the question of abstraction: Hunhu/Ubuntu speaks with great power about interconnectedness, solidarity and communal dignity, but translating those values into the specific, enforceable rules that AI governance requires is exquisitely hard work. Finally, the individualism embedded in AI reflects values that urbanisation and modernity have spread widely, including across Africa itself. A Hunhu/Ubuntu framework would need to reckon with that complexity.

What is needed, above all, is a dialogue, a genuine renegotiation of the values that AI exemplifies. Fortunately, the philosophical inspiration for that conversation exists: we have only to turn, once again, to the proverbs – Rume rimwe harikombi churu – one person cannot surround an anthill. The task of building an AI that works for all of humanity is a collective one.

item.title: Ani Liu: eye heart womb
item.dc:creator: Aeon Video
item.description:
A scientist, artist and mother, Ani Liu contemplates how power and control shape the body in her taboo-breaking artworks

- by Aeon Video

Watch on Aeon
item.content:encoded: For the widely exhibited US artist Ani Liu, the body is a site of mystery and data in equal measure. Drawing on a background that spans art, design and biotechnology, she works with what she calls ‘culturally loaded bodily materials’ such as sperm and breast milk to contemplate and expose ingrained ideas about gender, motherhood and labour. In this short film for PBS, the filmmaker Miao Wang follows Liu in the late stages of her third pregnancy as she develops new work. The film situates her practice within both personal history and wider social debates, including those surrounding reproductive rights in the United States. It also makes for a compelling introduction to an artist whose work challenges taboos, raising pressing questions at the intersection of the human body and technology.
